papers.summary: Environmental monitoring is crucial for addressing challenges related to climate change,water resource management, and disaster risk mitigation. This study advances the application of machine learning techniques for anomaly detection and forecasting of temperature and groundwater, focusing on temperature anomalies in Ticino, Switzerland, and groundwater level (GWL) fluctuations in Mendatica and Triora, Italy. By integrating these two domains, this research develops a scalable and accurate approach to enhance real-time environmental monitoring. Hydrometeorological data often exhibit complex, non-linear relationships that conventional statistical models struggle to capture. This study employs advanced machine learning models, including Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), and the Prophet model,to enhance real-time anomaly detection and forecasting. Additionally, statistical models and machine learning models such as Auto-Regressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA),Seasonal ARIMA (SARIMA), Support Vector Machine (SVM) and Recurrent Nerural Network-Gated Recurrent Unit (RNN-GRU) are utilized to provide a comparative assessment of traditional forecasting techniques against machine learning-based approaches. The methodological framework significantly improves predictive capabilities, with broad applications in disaster preparedness, water resource management, and climate change adaptation. The research methodology follows a structured approach, beginning with data collection from temperature sensors in Ticino, and piezometers in Mendatica and Triora. The acquired data undergo preprocessing to remove inconsistencies, ensuring high-quality input for analysis. A machine learning-driven anomaly detection framework is implemented to identify outliers in time-series data. papers.title: Current state and features of landslide process development within the territory of Dnipro city and Dnipropetrovsk region
papers.source: Bridges and tunnels Theory Research Practice
papers.summary: Purpose of the research is to analyse the current state of landslide-prone territories in Dnipro city and Dnipropetrovsk region, identify the main natural and technogenic factors controlling the development and activation of landslide processes, and substantiate the necessity for further research into the stability of soil slopes within urbanised territories. Methodology. The research was carried out on the basis of a comprehensive analysis of literature sources, materials from the state monitoring of exogenous geological processes, engineering-geological, geomorphological, and hydrogeological materials, cartographic information, and statistical data on the development of landslide processes within the territory of Dnipro city and Dnipropetrovsk region. Methods of systematisation, comparative analysis, and data generalisation were applied to assess the current state of landslide-prone territories and identify the factors affecting slope stability. Findings. The current state of landslide process development in Dnipropetrovsk region and Dnipro city has been analysed, and the territories with the highest concentration of active and potentially hazardous landslides have been identified. It has been established that the activation of landslide processes is caused by the combined influence of natural factors, including geological structure, relief, hydrogeological conditions, erosion processes, and climatic factors, as well as technogenic impacts associated with urban development, disturbance of natural drainage conditions, leakage from engineering networks, and uncontrolled surface runoff. Information on the most hazardous landslide sites has been generalised, and cases of large-scale landslide activation that occurred within the territory of Dnipro city have been analysed. Originality. papers.title: From Catastrophe to Legislation: The Payatas Dumpsite and the Transition to Ecological Solid Waste Management
papers.summary: The 2000 Payatas landfill collapse in Quezon City, Philippines in which hundreds of people were crushed by an avalanche of trash after a landslide at a landfill created by illegal trash disposal was a critical destabilizing event that changed the solid waste governance regime for the Philippines. It led to the passing of Republic Act 9003 (Ecological Solid Waste Management Act). Twenty plus years have passed since this event and while there has been progress towards ecological solid waste management it is still incomplete. Progress occurred at the National Level through legislation, however, local governments continue to struggle implementing the law due to ongoing practices of open dumping, and continued marginalization of community based actors.This study examines the Payatas transition as a case of sustainability in the Philippines utilizing four theories from transition management literature: (1) governance principles of diversity, dynamics & complexity; (2) The Transition Management Cycle that includes arena-building, visioning, experimentation & monitoring; (3) The X-Curve Framework developed by Hebinck et al. (2022), analyzing the case along the paths of Breakdown/Buildup and evaluating the composite regime strength score for each pathway; and (4) Evaluating government, market & community coordinating mechanisms. Results indicate persistent deficits in co-production among stakeholders, long-standing capacity shortfalls in funding and technical capabilities on the part of LGUs, low utilization of the knowledge and skills provided by informal waste sector workers, and lack of formally established multi-stakeholder transition arenas. papers.title: Harnessing Artificial Intelligence for Advancing Hydropower Development in Nepal
papers.summary: This paper discusses and reviews the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) in the development of hydropower project in Nepal. Nepal has immense potential in hydropower and significant energy resources, which could strengthen the energy sector, increase GDP and support the sustainable economic growth. The use of AI in this field could drive innovation in hydropower and water resource management. AI can be applied to the study of river morphology, hydrology, sedimentation, debris flow, landslides and the risk of lake or dam outburst floods. Case from Nepal show that the emerging use of AI in hydropower. However, its wider adoption will improved data availability, better sensor networks, enhance technical capacity and stronger institutional support.

papers.title: EERI Virtual Earthquake Reconnaissance Team (VERT): Phase 1 Response to the M7.7 Pitaloza Arriba, Panama Earthquake, October 9, 2026, in EERI 2026 Pitaloza Arriba, Panama Earthquake Reconnaissance
papers.summary: This report describes reconnaissance findings which were conducted virtually as part of the Earthquake Engineering Research Institute's (EERI) Learning from Earthquakes (LFE) Virtual Earthquakes Reconnaissance Team (VERT). VERT is a team of volunteers that activate after major earthquakes to curate reports on the impact to the community. VERT activates in a series of phases after an earthquake to assist in-field teams with data-driven reconnaissance. This report is VERT's Phase 1 report for the M7.7 Pitaloza Arriba, Panama earthquake that occurred on October 9th, 2026. The report summarizes earthquake characteristics, aftershocks, and emergency response, as well as geotechnical hazards such as tsunami and landslide impacts. The report also summarizes the impacts to the region on a variety of different topics, including public health, schools, buildings, housing, transportation, and utilities. This report is based on publicly available data after the events. The assessment provided in the report is performed by the judgment of the authors with limited access to ground-truthing. Data in this report are intended to give a rapid overview of earthquake impacts and inform potential field reconnaissance efforts.

papers.title: Editorial: Big data mining and artificial intelligence in earth science
papers.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) for geoscience uses intelligent algorithms to extract concealed patterns from big Earth data, enabling more accurate predictions and decisions in scientific discoveries and applications, such as Earth's evolution, geological modeling, environmental monitoring, hazard mitigation, and resource exploration (Zhou et al., 2018(Zhou et al., , 2026)). Its evolution has followed a clear paradigm transition-from early expert systems through data-driven machine learning, to the current physics-informed, knowledge-data dual-driven approaches (Zhou et al., 2018;Zuo et al., 2023;Cheng et al., 2025). This progression is not merely incremental; it is fundamentally reshaping geoscience by integrating big data analytics with machine learning algorithms, and in doing so, redefining the practices of many researchers and engineers in their daily work (Zuo et al., 2023;Zhou et al., 2026). This is the reason why this special topic issue comes to exist here. It is devoted to showcase recent advances in the research and application of AI across many geoscience disciplines. It highlights innovative methodologies in data science, machine learning, and 2 / 14 generative AI technologies that address the integration and interpretation of multidisciplinary geoscientific data.The special issue is also initiated to commemorates the 10th anniversary of the Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Big Data for Geosciences, established under the Chinese Society for Mineralogy, Petrology and Geochemistry in 2016, with Professor Zhou Yongzhang, then the awardee of the IAMG Felix Chayes Prize, as its inaugural Chair (Zhou et al., 2026). This marked the first organized effort in China to promote AI and big data research in mineralogy, petrology and geochemistry, and was among the earliest such professional bodies worldwide. papers.title: Worth waiting for, hardly worth waiting: data latency and the timing of regional landslide warnings in China
papers.summary: Abstract. Landslide warning services must weigh the better evidence that later data bring against the lead time lost while waiting for them. We studied this trade-off for 280 rainfall-induced landslides in China (2015–2024) with minute-, hour- or period-level occurrence times reported in the news, using the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission's Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for GPM (IMERG) precipitation and as-issued Global Forecast System (GFS) forecasts in a latency-aware retrospective replay. In a case-crossover design, observed rainfall replacing forecasts added substantial information (matched area under the receiver operating characteristic curve +0.058 [0.034, 0.081]), whereas later satellite runs and newer forecast cycles added little or none. In a rolling replay of 24 h warnings, waiting one 6 h step before issuing gave no stable gain in detection at warning loads of 0.5–10 % of cell-time. In a cost–loss analysis, issuing at once with satellite rainfall plus forecast reached a relative economic value (REV, dimensionless) of 0.55, close to a latency-free benchmark (0.57) and above a rainfall threshold (0.34) and, on matched 2015–2020 decisions, the archived version 2.0.0 Landslide Hazard Assessment for Situational Awareness (LHASA) nowcast (0.34). A value-of-information waiting rule added +0.002 [−0.005, +0.007] over the best fixed policy, averaged across the exploratory cost–loss range. The pre-specified cost–loss test could not discriminate, because almost no rule warns at its cost–loss ratios, but a second test, fixed before an independent 2008–2014 sample was assembled, detected a value of waiting when no forecast was available (+0.03 [0.01, 0.05] in REV). Brackets give 95 % confidence intervals. With both satellite rainfall and forecasts available, waiting rarely repaid its lead-time cost.

Dissemination of Electrical Resistivity Tomography (ERT) Investigation Results as a Landslide Mitigation Measure in the Batu Panggal Area, Samarinda
papers.source: ANDIL Mulawarman Journal of Community Engagement
papers.summary: Batu Panggal is an area in Loa Bakung Subdistrict, Samarinda, that has been repeatedly hit by landslides. The hilly morphology, high rainfall, and residential activities increase the vulnerability of this area to disasters. The main challenges faced by the community are the limited scientific information regarding subsurface conditions and the low capacity of residents to understand the causes of landslides and science-based mitigation measures. This Community Service Program aimed to enhance community understanding through the dissemination of Electrical Resistivity Tomography (ERT) geophysical survey results by utilizing a method traditionally employed for technical investigations as a science-based disaster education and risk communication tool for the community. The activity was conducted through presentations, discussions, and questionnaire-based evaluations to assess the community’s level of understanding and perception regarding the application of the ERT method for landslide management in Batu Panggal. The materials presented included the causes of landslides, the working principles of the ERT method, the interpretation of ERT survey results, and recommendations for landslide mitigation in the Batu Panggal area. The ERT survey results revealed the presence of low-resistivity zones (<50 ohm.m), indicating water-saturated layers and potential slip surfaces that may act as triggering factors for landslides. Questionnaire results showed that 100% of participants had no prior knowledge of the ERT method before the activity was conducted. However, after the dissemination session, all participants (100%) agreed that the ERT method could support landslide prevention and mitigation measure.. Furthermore, 59% of participants considered the ERT method beneficial, while 41% rated it as highly beneficial for landslide mitigation in their area. papers.title: Sequential high-density radiocarbon dating to detect invisible event layers in marine sediments
papers.summary: Abstract We present a unique application of radiocarbon measurements on hemipelagic sediments that uses continuous radiocarbon dating of total organic carbon ( 14 C TOC age) to recognize event deposits. The 14 C TOC age of sediments is not commonly used for age determination because total organic carbon includes various origins, such as marine, terrestrial, and reworked old fragments. In this study, the 14 C TOC ages of some horizons were found to be older than those of the deeper ones through continuous 14 C TOC measurements at 0.5- to 1.0-cm intervals. The reversal 14 C TOC ages resulted not from the settlement of organic particles from the terrestrial environments, such as floodings, but from the submarine slope failures. Therefore, we can regard the reversal 14 C TOC layers as event layers due to geohazards. After reconstruction of the age model using foraminiferal tests obtained from the sediment core used in this study, depositional ages of event layers were identified. Well correlation with historical natural disasters after the 15 th century suggest validity of the method proposed by the current study.

papers.title: Reconstructing Landslide Erosion Volumes from Post-Event Topography
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Landslide volume controls hillslope sediment budgets, but measuring it requires a pre-event high-resolution digital terrain model (DTM), which is rarely available. We reconstruct the pre-event surface inside scars from a single post-event lidar DTM and scar outlines. Rim interpolation gives a first surface, and a gradient-boosted model restores the slope convexity that interpolation cannot represent. Trained on real and synthetic scars on unfailed slopes, it predicts erosion only where terrain shows evidence of it. Using 1 m lidar from before and after the 2018 Hokkaido Eastern Iburi earthquake, cross-validated volumes for 1,708 landslides are within 2.5% of the measured total, with a median per-landslide error of 16%, and 0.1 m spurious depth on unfailed ground. At Iburi and at an independent test site, extending masks to intact ground recovered volumes reliably from a single post-event DTM. We provide the training and testing data in this repository along with the python code for reconstructions.

papers.title: Australia: Political developments and data in 2025 – Labor landslide, Coalition collapse
papers.source: European Journal of Political Research Political Data Yearbook
papers.summary: Abstract This article examines key political developments in Australia during 2025, an election year. The databook entry covers results from the 2025 Landslide re-election of the incumbent Australian Labor Party and their aftermath. Regional elections in two jurisdictions, where both incumbents were returned, as well as a federal Cabinet reshuffle and institutional changes which reformed campaign finance and donations are also discussed. The gender composition of the Federal parliament improved, largely on the back of Labor’s huge majority. The party system faced pressure with the Coalition’s record low election performance, and record performance for Independents and minor parties. National policy issues centred on persistent cost-of-living pressures, including inflation and housing and environmental law reforms. Foreign policy challenges included the Gaza conflict, managing Australia’s relationship with China and continued commitment to the AUKUS submarine programme.

papers.title: A hybrid negative sampling strategy for landslide susceptibility assessment in mining area
papers.summary: Reliable delineation of non-landslide samples remains a challenge in data-driven landslide susceptibility assessment, particularly where landslide inventories are incomplete. This study proposes a hybrid negative sampling (HNS) strategy that integrates frequency ratio (FR)-based susceptibility pre-screening with SPY-based positive–unlabeled (PU) learning and differentiated instance weighting. Specifically, an initial pool of fuzzy negatives was derived from frequency ratio-based susceptibility indices, followed by the SPY algorithm to identify relatively high-confidence negative candidates. The integration of these two sources allows candidate negatives with different screening confidence levels to contribute to model training through distinct weights. Applied to Jiaokou County, a loess mining area in China (157 inventory-positive geological hazard records, 1,914 slope units), the methodology was evaluated using a common five-fold spatial holdout validation protocol with XGBoost and SVM, four baseline sampling strategies, and positive-to-negative ratios of 1:1 and 1:2. HNS achieved the highest mean ROC-AUC across all four classifier–ratio configurations, including 0.812 ± 0.041 for XGBoost and 0.797 ± 0.055 for SVM at 1:2, although its improvements over baseline strategies were modest and not statistically significant. Sensitivity and ablation analyses indicated that differentiated weighting primarily influenced the trade-offs among Recall, Precision, and Specificity, without consistently improving overall discrimination or area-based capture performance. Furthermore, SHAP analysis identified fractional vegetation cover (FVC), nighttime lights (NTL), and lithology as the leading contributors to model predictions rather than direct causal factors. Overall, HNS provides a structured approach to incorporating candidate negatives with different screening confidence levels, offering competitive predictive performance with application-dependent benefits and trade-offs.

papers.title: Slope Units produced from Slope Unit Maker (SUMak) over the contiguous United States, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico
papers.summary: Slope units divide terrain by drainage and divide lines to create mapping units that capture individual hillslopes. Using the software slope unit maker (SUMak) (Woodard, 2023), we delineated slope units across the contiguous United States, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico that are scaled to the fluvial-hillslope threshold (Woodard et al., 2024). Data are organized according to their respective watershed hydrologic unit codes (HUC). The HUC watersheds are designed so that lower-order watersheds (e.g., HUC 4) nest within higher-order watersheds (e.g., HUC 2). The parent directories in this repository are named after the HUC 2 watersheds, and their subfolders are named after the HUC 4 watersheds. Each HUC 4 subfolder contains shapefiles of the delineated stream network, intermediate basins, and slope units. We aggregated all the results of the HUC 8 processed data into one file for each feature within the HUC 4. Shapefiles that show the extent of the HUC watersheds are available at U.S. Geological Survey (2025). Files are named by the HUC 4 code, followed by ‘streams’, ‘intBasins’, and ‘slopeUnits’, for the streams, intermediate basins, and slope units, respectively (e.g., ‘0202intBasins.shp’). References cited: U.S. Geological Survey, 2025, USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset (WBD), accessed January 10, 2025, at https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/index.html?prefix=StagedProducts/Hydrography/WBD/National/GDB/. papers.title: LiDAR-Constrained Multi-Temporal UAV Monitoring of Glacier Terminus Retreat and Secondary Landslide Evolution at Hailuogou Glacier, Mt. Gongga, China
papers.summary: Joint quantification of glacier terminus change and adjacent secondary landslide evolution can be challenging when multi-temporal UAV datasets lack a consistent absolute spatial reference, thereby limiting robust assessment of their stage-dependent covariation. This study investigated the Hailuogou glacier terminus and the Laoguanjingtai (LGJT) landslide using six UAV photogrammetric surveys acquired between 2018 and 2022 and synchronous airborne light detection and ranging (LiDAR) data from 2022. LiDAR reference constraints and elevation-residual assessment over relatively stable terrain supported multi-temporal digital elevation model (DEM) differencing. The glacier terminus area decreased from 2.63×105m2 to 1.43×105m2, representing a reduction of 45.5%. From July 2020 to August 2022, the glacier volume ablation rate reached 1.00×106m3a−1. Meanwhile, the LGJT landslide shifted from deposition-dominated adjustment from 2018 to 2019 to erosion-dominated material export after July 2020, when its erosion rate reached 3.73×105m3a−1 and its net volume change rate decreased to −3.39×105m3a−1. Annualized rates across five unequal intervals showed positive covariation between glacier ablation and landslide erosion and negative covariation with net landslide volume change. These exploratory associations, together with the spatial concentration of elevation change near the glacier–landslide margin, are consistent with a geomorphic linkage. The LiDAR-constrained UAV workflow provides a practical basis for integrated monitoring of glacier retreat and adjacent sediment redistribution.

papers.title: Effects of climate change on hydrogeological hazard: the case of the Niscemi landslides (Southern Sicily, Italy)
papers.summary: Abstract This study analyzes precipitation variability and the hydrometeorological conditions associated with extreme hydrogeological events in the Niscemi area (southern Sicily), combining historical series (1885–2020), ERA5 data, and future projections of rainfall intensity. The comparison between the hydrogeological events of October 12, 1997, and January 26, 2026 highlights how such events can develop through different hydrometeorological configurations, yet are both preceded by high soil moisture conditions, confirming the key role of antecedent precipitation and its temporal distribution. The climatic analysis shows that cumulative precipitation does not exhibit a significant linear trend but is strongly modulated by Euro-Mediterranean atmospheric circulation, with significant negative correlations with EA (ρ = -0.74) and MOI (ρ = -0.66), and more moderate correlations with NAO and WeMO. In contrast, mean rainfall intensity shows an increasing trend over time and is only weakly correlated with the indices, with a significant relationship observed only with WeMO (ρ = -0.34). The intensification is also associated with synoptic configurations characterized by positive NAO. Projections obtained using a SARIMAX model, forced with SSP scenarios, indicate a progressive increase in rainfall intensity throughout the 21st century, reaching up to approximately 40% under high-emission scenarios. Overall, the results highlight that extreme hydrogeological events arise from the interaction between atmospheric circulation variability, thermodynamic conditions, and antecedent rainfall conditions, emphasizing the need for integrated approaches to risk assessment in a climate change context.

A unified model embedding MCC-MLD constitutive laws in Biot’s framework for settlement of Weinan interbedded clay-sand loess foundations
papers.summary: Consolidation settlement prediction in interbedded clay–sand loess foundations is complicated by stratigraphic heterogeneity and hydromechanical coupling that homogeneous-soil models cannot capture. This study presents an integrated elastoplastic framework combining the Modified Cam-Clay model for loessial clay, the Wright–Duncan model for sand with particle breakage, and Biot’s consolidation theory in a unified implementation for the Weinan plain, China. Parameters for clay, sand, and transitional interlayers came from 20 borehole samples. Although each component is established, their integration with site-specific enhancements—a structure-dependent yield surface for shallow clay and a breakage-dependent hardening law for deep sand—constitutes a practical advancement. The numerical implementation via Python-Matlab, validated against borehole data from the same site using a reserved validation set (6 boreholes not used in calibration), reveals settlement in three stages—elastic rebound, primary consolidation (70–80% of total), and secondary creep—peaking at the 20–30 m clay–sand interface, where sand dilatancy transfers 12–18% of stress to clay, quantified by the proposed γ–μ interface parameter system. Spatially, settlement is shallow-dominated with deep-layer lag; temporally, sand accelerates clay pore-pressure dissipation by 35–40%. The model attains ± 5% accuracy versus ± 25% for homogenization and establishes a closed-loop monitoring–inversion–updating workflow. Assuming full saturation, it neglects matric-suction effects in the vadose zone, including water-table fluctuations and dry–wet cycles. At the Weinan site (water table 15–25 m), the model applies directly to deep saturated strata, contributing most (70–80%) of consolidation settlement; the shallow unsaturated zone requires caution and further characterization.

papers.title: AI-Powered Drones for Disaster Search and Rescue: A Review of Human Detection, Autonomous Navigation and Emergency Communication
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Earthquakes, floods, landslides and building collapses cause serious damage and loss of life, and locating trapped or stranded people quickly is one of the most critical tasks for rescue teams. Ground searches are slow and often dangerous in unstable or inaccessible areas. AI-powered drones offer a faster and safer alternative by combining aerial mobility with onboard cameras, thermal sensors, GPS and computer vision. This paper reviews the design of AI drones for disaster rescue. It examines aerial datasets and deep object detectors for recognizing people, vehicles and damaged structures from above, thermal imaging for finding victims at night or under light cover, coverage path planning for searching large areas systematically, simultaneous localization and mapping for operation where GPS is unreliable, and drone networks that relay communication when ground infrastructure fails. Practical constraints of battery life, payload, onboard computing and regulation are discussed. A five-layer architecture comprising sensing, onboard edge AI, navigation and control, communication and a ground control station is proposed, followed by a research gap analysis, objectives, comparison of detection models and a discussion of challenges. The review concludes that AI drones can cover large areas quickly, reach inaccessible locations and reduce risk to rescuers, making disaster response faster, safer and more effective.

papers.title: Framing Disasters and Environmental Injustice in Underserved Communities
papers.summary: Disasters come in many forms, and all are evolving into more violent forms of themselves. There are many types of natural disasters , including hurricanes, flooding, landslides, wildfires, and others. Man-made disasters have impacted humanity and all forms of life on Earth. Then, there are environmental polluting disasters , which are a double-barreled calamity. It wreaks havoc and chaos in two ways, and it destroys the quality of life for humans, via cancer and other debilitating illnesses that shorten the life expectancy of mankind, while causing global warming, coastal erosion, and fueling the strength of hurricanes, tornadoes, and snowstorms. This chapter introduces and sets the tone for the remaining chapters in the book. It provides an overview of the various types of disasters and environmental injustices that often affect underserved communities with more severe consequences. This chapter prompts the reader to ponder the responsibilities of federal, state, and local governments in overseeing and directing federal assistance programs to equip and support disadvantaged populations as they become more independent and able to help themselves.

papers.title: Integrating machine-learning-based landslide susceptibility and vulnerability for slope-unit risk assessment
papers.source: Journal of risk analysis and crisis response
papers.summary: Landslide susceptibility identifies terrain associated with landslide occurrence, whereas risk prioritization also requires information on the vulnerability of threatened elements. This letter presents a slope-unit framework linking machine-learning susceptibility prediction, SHAP-based interpretation, and vulnerability-based relative risk classification. Four models were evaluated using a regional test dataset, and the selected model was applied to 393 slope units. XGBoost achieved the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC = 0.952), followed by random forest (0.904), logistic regression (0.662), and support vector machine (0.600). Paired DeLong tests indicated significant differences between XGBoost and logistic regression (LR) and support vector machine (SVM), but not random forest (RF). SHAP analysis identified slope, relief, and elevation as the leading predictors, accounting for 62.83% of normalized grouped importance. High and very high relative risk occupied 21.34% of the mapped slope-unit area. Of 69 very-high-susceptibility units, only 13 were classified as very high risk after vulnerability integration. The framework supports the identification of priority slope units for targeted field investigation, monitoring, and mitigation planning.

papers.title: Quantifying the long-term evolution of post-earthquake debris-flow activity in the epicentral area of the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake, China
papers.summary: Abstract The 2008 Wenchuan earthquake triggered widespread coseismic landslides and supplied large volumes of loose material on hillslopes and channels, resulting in persistent post-earthquake debris flow activity near the epicentral area. Quantifying the long-term evolution of this activity is important for geohazard assessment, but remains challenge because debris flows are jointly controlled by sediment supply, topography, and rainfall. In this study, a catchment-scale framework was developed to evaluate debris flow activity intensity in 44 catchments affected by the Wenchuan earthquake. Multi-temporal landslide inventories from 2008 to 2019 were used to calculate landslide sediment supply potential (LSSP), which integrates landslide areal density, spatial distribution indices, and channel gradient. LSSP was then combined with representative hourly rainfall intensities from documented debris flow triggering events to derive a debris flow activity intensity index (AI DF ). The results show that active landslide area decreased from 122.05 km² in 2008 to 30.55 km² in 2019, while recovery areas expanded progressively. LSSP increased sharply immediately after the earthquake and then declined over time, with a rapid decrease during 2008–2011 followed by a slower adjustment phase. Nevertheless, sediment supply in many catchments remained above the pre-earthquake level in 2019. AI DF showed an overall decline after its post-earthquake peak, although temporary increases occurred during major rainfall events. Comparison with documented debris flow events indicates that AI DF captures the main temporal pattern of observed activity. The fitted long-term trend suggests three stages of post-earthquake debris flow activity: an active period from 2008 to 2013, a recession period from 2013 to 2048, and a relatively stable period after 2048. These results indicate that debris flow activity in the Wenchuan earthquake-affected area may persist for several decades, mainly controlled

papers.title: Landslideagent with multimodal landslidebench: a domain-rule-augmented agent for autonomous landslide identification and analysis
papers.summary: Intelligent identification and analysis of landslides are critical for disaster prevention. However, current interpretation paradigms struggle to simultaneously extract visual features and geoscientific semantics, while general-purpose vision–language models (VLMs) suffer from perceptual limitations and domain hallucinations in complex geological scenarios. This paper proposes an instruction-driven agentic framework for landslide response that integrates a multimodal benchmark, a specialized VLM, and a rule-enhanced agent. First, a multimodal fine-grained landslide dataset LandslideBench with seven landslide subtype labels, high-resolution imagery, pixel-level masks, and high-quality textual descriptions is constructed through multi-VLM cross-validation and interactive annotation. Second, a landslide-oriented dual-head vision-language method, LandslideVLM, is proposed and fine-tuned on LandslideBench via low-rank adaptation, in which a discriminative classification head and a generative language head are integrated to jointly support fine-grained landslide classification and geoscientific semantic description. Finally, a domain-rule-enhanced LandslideAgent is developed by integrating structured report metadata constraints and cross-validation identification constraints. Experimental results demonstrate that LandslideBench can serve as an effective benchmark for landslide interpretation. The fine-tuned LandslideVLM achieves accuracy improvements of 12.79%, 55.71%, and 17.27% on landslide discrimination, fine-grained classification, and semantic description quality, respectively. Across 28 paired cases, rule-constrained LandslideAgent achieves an accuracy of 88.7% across six evidence-checkable fields, outperforming free-mode agent by 11.9%.

papers.title: Cloudbursts and Floods in Nepal: Ecological Pathways, Evidence Gaps, and Consequences for Aquatic Fauna and Freshwater Ecosystems
papers.source: Journal of Global Agriculture and Ecology
papers.summary: This review assesses how cloudburst-associated flash floods, monsoon floods, and sediment-laden cascading floods impact aquatic fauna and freshwater ecosystems in Nepal. A synthesis of original research was conducted to connect hydroclimatic and geomorphic data to field observations of benthic macroinvertebrates, macrophytes, fishes, crocodilians, and river dolphins. Periodic monsoon flooding does not automatically equate to ecological degradation. For example, Nepalese stream invertebrates are capable of exhibiting population-level flexibility, and flood pulses are known to maintain channel-floodplain connectivity. However, the potential for degradation increases when rainfall, landslide sediment, and bank failure are combined with anthropogenic flooding. Buried fauna and flora experience both habitat homogenisation and disconnection during recovery. The strongest Nepal-specific evidence is for macroinvertebrate seasonality and habitat controls; direct indicators of the effects of cloudbursts on aquatic ecosystems are largely lacking. Post-flood surveys conducted in Koshi Tappu document the displacement and alteration of habitats of fauna, but do not support either mortality or biodiversity loss on a national scale. Fish and river dolphin studies have shown the importance of habitat depth, discharge, water quality, habitat connectivity, and dry season refuges on the fauna of aquatic ecosystems. The objective of this study is to assess how cloudburst-associated flash floods, monsoon floods, and sediment-laden cascading floods affect aquatic fauna and the ecological integrity of freshwater ecosystems in Nepal. The State of Nepal should use hydrometeorology and sediment measurements to guide before-after-control-impact studies of the effects of hazard mitigation practices. The conservation goal should be to protect aquatic ecosystems from fragmentation caused by emergency flood protection systems.

papers.title: Record warmth in the Sea of Japan amplified the September 2024 Noto heavy rainfall associated with a mesoscale low-pressure disturbance
papers.summary: Abstract In September 2024, record-breaking rainfall caused severe flooding and landslides in the Noto region, Japan, where recovery from the devastating Noto Peninsula earthquake was still ongoing. During this event, the Sea of Japan experienced record warmth, with monthly-mean sea surface temperature anomaly of + 2.9 °C. To quantify the impact of this anomalous ocean warming on the heavy rainfall, we conducted numerical sensitivity experiments using a regional atmospheric model in which only the sea surface temperature conditions in the Sea of Japan were replaced with those from each year between 1991 and 2020. Simulated rainfall over the Noto region was nearly twice as large under the observed 2024 SST conditions, indicating that the exceptionally warm ocean substantially amplified the event. The warming did not alter the occurrence or track of a mesoscale low-pressure disturbance along the autumn rain front, but the intensity of the disturbance systematically increased with SST and was accompanied by stronger southwesterly winds and moisture transport into the frontal zone. Ocea​nic analyses further showed a marked strengthening of the Tsushima Warm Current in 2024. These results highlight the importance of atmospheric responses to anomalously warm ocean conditions in amplifying extreme rainfall under anomalously warm ocean conditions and underscore the need to consider such processes in future risk assessments around Japan.

papers.title: Geomorphic calibration of friction and entrainment parameters for a snowmelt-induced muddy debris flow in the Longiarù Valley, Dolomites
papers.summary: Abstract Snowmelt- and rainfall-triggered debris flows are important geomorphic hazards in alpine environments, yet frictional and entrainment parameters are rarely available for individual events. This study constrains these parameters for a snowmelt-induced muddy debris flow that occurred in the Seres Creek catchment, Longiarù Valley, Dolomites, on 17–18 June 2024. A pre-event DEM from 2010 and a post-event LiDAR-derived DEM from 2024 were used to derive a DEM of Difference (DoD) and characterize the spatial distribution of erosion and deposition associated with the event. The observed geomorphic response was then used to constrain the internal friction, basal friction, turbulent friction, and entrainment parameters through iterative r.avaflow simulations. The calibrated parameter combination comprised an internal friction angle of 17°, a basal friction angle of 9°, a turbulent friction parameter of 10 m/s², and an entrainment coefficient of kg⁻¹. The resulting simulation reproduced the major spatial characteristics of the observed event, including the transition from erosion and channel incision in the upper and intermediate reaches to deposition downstream. Comparisons of selected turbulent friction and entrainment values showed that turbulent friction strongly affected flow mobility, erosion, and runout, whereas entrainment substantially influenced flow momentum, erosion, and the downstream position of deposition. Comparison of simulated and DoD-derived geomorphic changes along the main flow path and at three representative cross-sections showed good spatial agreement in the major erosion–deposition patterns, with relatively minor localized differences in erosion and deposition magnitude. The results show that spatially distributed geomorphic change can provide constraints on frictional and entrainment parameters beyond runout extent alone, providing a spatially informed basis for event-scale debris-flow modelling.

papers.title: Queer Resistance and Gender Fluidity in Nepali Short Stories
papers.summary: This research chapter studies the struggles of sexual minorities in contemporary Nepali short stories: Usha Sherchan’s Unexpected Flood and Landslide , Archana Thapa’s Bimarda (“Effeminate”) taken from the anthologies Tesro Rang , and Kathaputala respectively, and Samrat Upadhyay’s The Royal Ghosts , the title story from the anthology The Royal Ghosts . In these literary narratives, the central characters recurrently deviate from the conventional gender roles and identities. They refuse to be confined to the socially imposed gender identities of heterosexual males or females. The deviation leads them to miserable condition as they are obligated to face various forms of discrimination. Based on this problem, this study explores the reasons behind their deviation from conventional gender roles and identity, the consequences they face while dismantling the heterosexual gender identity, and the ways in which they subvert stereotypical gender expectations. Based on Judith Butler’s theory of gender performativity and Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick’s critique of binary sexual categories, this chapter argues that gender is not an inherent trait, but a socially constructed identity. Individual’s gender is shaped through his/her performance and reinforced by cultural and societal norms. Butler and Sedgwick argue that individual’s gender identity is fluid, performative, and socially regulated. Through this theoretical lens, the current research concludes that the central characters in the selected texts resist and redefine traditional gender norms. They endure fear, humiliation, and abuse due to the intolerant attitude toward the queer identity within the Nepali socio-cultural context.

papers.title: LaRaTh-Br: An Event-Based Probabilistic Framework for Modeling Rainfall Conditions Associated with Landslides
papers.summary: Rainfall-based models are widely used to support territorial landslide early warning systems, in which the occurrence of one or more landslides is assessed over predefined warning areas rather than at individual, known slopes. Their development, however, is strongly influenced by methodological choices related to rainfall-event definition, rainfall–landslide association, predictor construction, and model calibration, especially when operational landslide inventories contain uncertainties in the timing and location of reported events. Here, we present LaRaTh-Br (Landslide Rainfall Thresholds—Brazil), a modular R-based computational framework designed to standardize event-based rainfall–landslide analysis. The framework integrates rainfall-event identification from continuous precipitation records, spatial and temporal association between rainfall events and landslide records, generation of multiple rainfall descriptors, and probabilistic modelling and validation. LaRaTh-Br adopts the rainfall event as the fundamental analytical unit and explicitly represents both events associated and not associated with reported landslides. The framework was demonstrated through a retrospective event-level modelling application using ten years of operational rainfall observations and landslide records from Blumenau, southern Brazil. The application showed that event duration and mean rainfall intensity contained most of the discriminatory information, while antecedent rainfall provided complementary information and short-duration peak intensity produced limited additional gain. More importantly, LaRaTh-Br enables alternative rainfall-event definitions, rainfall descriptors, and modelling configurations to be evaluated within a common and reproducible workflow, providing a flexible basis for the continued development and refinement of probabilistic rainfall–landslide models as operational rainfall and landslide datasets expand in Brazil and elsewhere.

papers.title: Data and Code for: From Intention to Adoption: Climate Change Adaptation among Farmers in Colombia’s Coffee-Growing Region
papers.summary: This repository contains the survey data and R replication code for the study “From Intention to Adoption: Climate Change Adaptation among Farmers in Central Colombia.” The dataset comprises survey responses from 360 smallholder farmers across 12 villages (veredas) in three departments of Colombia’s central region (Caldas, Quindío, and Risaralda, also known as the coffee-growing region), stratified by hazard history (drought, landslide, or no reported events) using records from Colombia’s National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD, 2005-2021). For each of seven climate change adaptation practices (water source protection, agroforestry, soil cover, retaining walls, income diversification, formal credit/insurance, and loans from non-financial sources), the data include Protection Motivation Theory constructs (perceived severity, perceived vulnerability, self-efficacy, response efficacy, perceived monetary and time costs, resistance to change), intention to adopt, and current adoption status, together with farm- and household-level control variables (age, gender, marital status, education, income, farm size, land ownership, number of workers, presence of water bodies o the farm, forest resources on the farm, and village-level hazard and altitude exposure). The accompanying R script (intention-adoption_script.R) reproduces all tables and appendices reported in the manuscript: a fractional-response model of adoption intention (Stage 1), a Bayesian multivariate probit model of joint adoption across five main practices, corrected for the endogeneity of intention via a control-function approach (Stage 2), and a full set of robustness checks, including an ordered-logit re-estimation, a wild cluster bootstrap, exclusion-restriction tests, and a village-block cluster bootstrap of the entire two-stage pipeline. A companion data dictionary (the Codebook and Location_Codes sheets in data.xlsx) documents the coding and exact survey wording of every variable.

papers.title: Improved Mask R-CNN inventory mapping and multivariable geo-environmental assessment of rainfall-induced shallow landslides in mountainous Beijing, China
papers.summary: Extreme rainfall can trigger numerous small, boundary-fragmented and spatially clustered shallow landslides. This study combined improved instance segmentation with reproducible spatial analysis to map and assess shallow landslides associated with the 2023 ‘23.7’ rainstorm in Zhaitang Town, mountainous Beijing. An improved Mask R-CNN integrated a convolutional block attention module, a path aggregation feature pyramid network and Soft-NMS. Under the random tile-level test design, the model achieved 89.51% precision, 88.31% recall, an F1 score of 88.91% and a mean intersection over union of 80.03%; these are in-scene estimates rather than evidence of geographic transferability. The resulting inventory contains 8298 landslides covering 3.05 km². Analysis of the harmonized geospatial layers showed that kernel density > 69.5 landslides/km² occupied 6.42% of the valid study area and contained 48.90% of mapped landslides. Frequency-ratio analysis identified enrichment in Wumishan Formation Members 1–3, 400–800 m elevation, 30–60° slopes, east-to-southwest aspects and concave terrain. A presence–background logistic model using 8212 landslide locations and 48,553 valid fixed-seed background samples showed no independent association for cumulative rainfall (odds ratio [OR] 1.00 per standard deviation, p = 0.999) or hourly intensity (OR 0.91, p = 0.407) after adjustment. Elevation, slope, plan curvature, aspect and lithology remained associated. Rainfall×slope and rainfall×susceptible-lithology interactions were non-significant. Residual Moran’s I was significant at 1 km but non-significant at 2–4 km aggregation, whereas five-fold spatial-block validation varied among regions (ROC AUC 0.699–0.870). The results separate event attribution from within-event spatial association and demonstrate a transparent workflow from rapid inventory mapping to spatially diagnosed environmental assessment.

papers.title: The impact of population growth on land-use: a system dynamics model for sustainable land-use planning in the Elgon Region of Uganda
papers.summary: Land-use and land-cover change poses major environmental challenge in regions where population growth increasingly drives encroachment into ecologically sensitive landscapes. This challenge arises from the dynamics of interacting feedbacks among; demographic change, declining household land size, ecosystem degradation, and delayed institutional responses. Previous studies in the context of Uganda, have investigated these factors, either independently or in pairs, but not holistically. This study developed a system dynamics model to examine the impact of population-driven land-use dynamics in the landslide prone Elgon region of Uganda. A System dynamics method was used to simulate long-term system behaviour under alternative policy intervention scenarios for sustainable land-use planning. Results indicate that the steady increase in the number of households and decline in land per household are the dominant drivers of encroachment into wetlands and forests. Population growth drives significant conversion of natural ecosystems, with forest cover declining from 317 km² in 2020 to 247 km² (22.08%) by 2050 under business-as-usual scenario, amidst rising demand for agricultural land, housing, fuelwood, and infrastructure. Wetland follows a similar trajectory, decreasing sharply from 47.7 km² to 28.3 km² (40.67%) over the same scenario. These trends are reinforced by weak institutional capacity, limited enforcement, low community participation, and inadequate coordination among conservation actors, which collectively undermine effective policy implementation. The findings also highlight the risks of business-as-usual land management and underscore the need for strengthened institutional enforcement, and coordinated conservation interventions. By explicitly capturing feedback-driven dynamics and long-term system responses, the model offers a policy-relevant decision-support tool for evaluating alternative interventions and guiding sustainable land-use planning in population

papers.title: ES&T Next 60 Years: Sustainability and Climate Change
Forest Composition Controls on Water Security in Nepal's Middle Hills
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Montane watersheds in the Himalayan region are becoming increasingly vulnerable to hydroclimatic extremes that cause floods, landslides, droughts and seasonal water scarcity. These risks are compounded by ecohydrological transformation resulting from shifts in forest composition, notably the widespread establishment of pine plantations, as well as climate variability and intensified land‐use activities. Understanding how forest composition influences watershed hydrological response remains a key challenge. Here, we use long‐term data and process‐based modelling of forest canopy trends to simulate ecohydrological dynamics in a headwater catchment supplying water to the Kathmandu Valley. The model is used to assess the hydrological performance of four forest composition scenarios: status quo (current forest cover), monoculture‐pine, monoculture‐broadleaf and managed‐mixed forest. The process‐based model, RHESSys, was used to evaluate seasonal evapotranspiration (ET), groundwater depth response, streamflow and canopy dynamics across scenarios. Given the uncertainty in climate forcing data and the strong topographic variability, the model reproduced observed daily streamflow reasonably well. Daily NSE, LNSE, KGE and PBIAS were 0.55, 0.65, 0.60 and 24% in calibration and 0.57, 0.72, 0.61 and 23% in validation, respectively. Monthly values were 0.61, 0.67, 0.64 and 24% in calibration and 0.68, 0.78, 0.66 and 23% in validation, respectively. Results show that pine‐dominated forests exhibit elevated year‐round water demand, and therefore lower low flows (lowest 1% of daily flows) by 7.7%. In contrast, broadleaf forests can reduce high flows (highest 1% of daily flows) by 4% while increasing low flows by 29% and reducing ET during water‐limited periods. However, the managed‐mixed forest scenario delivers the most balanced and sustainable hydrological performance, reducing high flows by 5% and increasing low flows by 16%. papers.title: Explainable Machine Learning for Multi-Temporal Landslide Detection along the Mechi– Tamor Corridor, Eastern Nepal"
papers.summary: Abstract This study explores a multi-temporal, multi-sensor framework for landslide detection along the Mechi Highway–Tamor River corridor in Ilam, Panchthar, Taplejung and Dhankuta districts of eastern Nepal. The framework is evaluated on two contrasting rainfall-triggered events, a late-monsoon withdrawal event in early October 2025 and a peak-monsoon event on 20 July 2026, which differ in rainfall intensity, duration, structure and antecedent wetness. An event-based inventory of 116 landslide scars was compiled through visual interpretation of Sentinel-2 imagery and cross-checked against a regional baseline of 255 landslide records. This inventory was combined with Sentinel-1 SAR backscatter change, optical spectral indices, terrain derivatives, antecedent rainfall and lithology to create a feature table of 410 units with 820 observations (unit × event). Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers were trained and evaluated under a naive random split and two spatially independent validation schemes (leave-one-municipality-out and spatial block cross-validation); the spatial schemes yielded F1 scores of 0.47–0.56 and ROC-AUC of 0.80–0.84, substantially lower than the optimistic random-split estimate (F1 = 0.77–0.80, ROC-AUC = 0.95), demonstrating the necessity of spatial validation for this problem. SHAP analysis showed that SAR backscatter change was the most important predictor overall, but that optical spectral indices, especially the Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR) difference, carried more signal wherever cloud-free images were available. SAR's value in this setting lies in cloud penetration rather than in superior predictive power. Combining predicted susceptibility with proximity to schools, health facilities and road bridges identified 35 critical corridor segments.

papers.title: Numerical Evaluation of Factor of Safety (FOS) and Anchor Pile Arrangement for Slope Stability Using GeoStudio (SLOPE/W)
papers.source: Progress in Engineering Application and Technology
papers.summary: Slope stability is an important issue that should be prioritized in construction engineering because unstable slopes can cause landslides, property damage and risks to human life. In Malaysia, slope failures often happen due to steep slope cuts and weak soil. This study investigates slope performance under different soil conditions, including poorly graded soils, medium‑dense sand, dense silty sand, well‑graded sands, and well‑compacted soils or rock, combined with varying slope angles of 30°, 60°, and 90°. This study used GeoStudio software (SLOPE/W) with the Morgenstern-Price method to find the Factor of Safety (FOS) and to propose and optimize anchor pile system arrangement that can improve slope stability for the condition examined with external load. The slope height is six meters, and three slope angles were studied, 30°, 60° and 90°. Soil properties such as cohesion (0 to 20 kPa) and friction angle (5° to 45°) were varied to evaluation their effects on slope stability. The results showed that poorly graded soils had very low FOS values, 0.130 indicating unstable conditions, while well-compacted soils and rocks gave higher FOS values, 2.897. Anchors pile system was installed at a downward angle of 10° and a spacing of 3 meters for all condition of soils. The anchors increased the FOS by acting on friction and providing pull-out resistance. For slopes of 30° and 60°, the effect of anchors shows increased stability and increased the FOS past the safe limit of 1.30, as required by the JKR Guidelines. However, for very steep slopes, found that anchors alone were not sufficient, the recommendation indicated that other methods, retaining structures were required. Overall, this study demonstrated that anchor pile reinforcement significantly improves slope stability for moderate slopes but is insufficient for vertical slopes where additional retaining systems are required.

papers.title: Research Progress on the Distribution Characteristics and Hazard-Inducing Effects of Macroscopic Interfaces in Loess Tableland Areas: With a Focus on Studies of the Southern Jingyang Tableland
papers.source: International Journal of Natural Resources and Environmental Studies
papers.summary: Macroscopic interfaces, including joints and fissures, interstratal contacts, paleosol horizons, and weak interlayers, are widespread in loess tableland areas. These interfaces alter slope integrity and stress-transfer pathways while influencing water infiltration, local water retention, and strength degradation. They therefore provide an important perspective for understanding the development and initiation of loess landslides. Drawing on previous research into loess discontinuities, rainfall infiltration, slope deformation and failure, physical model testing, and numerical simulation, this review systematically examines the classification and spatial development of macroscopic interfaces, their hydro-mechanical effects, discontinuity propagation, and slope instability modes. Research on the Southern Jingyang Tableland is used to evaluate existing agreements and limitations. Available evidence indicates that macroscopic interfaces affect loess slope stability by dissecting slope masses, promoting preferential infiltration, and modifying local stress conditions. However, consistent multiscale characterization of interface geometry, progressive coalescence under hydro-mechanical coupling, and quantitative relationships with landslide kinematics require further investigation. Future research directions are proposed to inform geohazard identification, assessment, and mitigation in loess tableland areas.

papers.title: Enhancing decision support system by prioritising critical areas in landslide disaster management of Kinnaur District, Himachal Pradesh
papers.summary: Abstract The Himalayan region is highly susceptible to landslides and has witnessed several fatal incidents in recent years. Implementing a priority-based ranking system for landslide management is essential to help decision-makers identify the most vulnerable or high-risk zones. This approach ensures that limited resources—such as funding, manpower, and technical expertise—are allocated efficiently. The prioritization process involves systematically evaluating and categorizing areas or projects based on the severity of risk, potential impact, and urgency of required interventions. By focusing on mitigation efforts, emergency preparedness, and infrastructure enhancement in the most at-risk zones, authorities can significantly reduce the likelihood of landslide-related disasters and strengthen community resilience. In this study, we propose a priority score ranking system for the Kinnaur district of Himachal Pradesh, based on the assessment of exposure levels of individual elements at risk, both in terms of landslide initiation and runout paths, along with their strategic importance. The resulting individual priority score maps and the integrated priority map are intended to support decision-making for a landslide early warning system and the effective allocation of resources for disaster risk reduction. Our findings indicate that approximately 5% area of the Kinnaur district should be prioritized for resource allocation to implement targeted mitigation strategies. This framework can be readily adapted on a regional scale for use in other landslide-prone regions to support focused planning and execution of disaster risk reduction initiatives.

papers.title: Exploring the Hydrological Functions and Effectiveness of Nature-based Solutions in Mountain Environments: Evidence, Indicators, and Comparability
papers.summary: Abstract. Mountain regions play a vital role in providing water resources, yet their hydrological systems are under threat from by climate change, land-use change, and socio-economic pressures. Although Nature-based solutions (NbS) are increasingly being considered as a means of ensuring water security, evidence of their hydrological performance in mountain environments is inconsistent and limited. This study presents a critical scoping review of the evidence on the hydrological functions of NbS in mountain regions, examining how reported hydrological effects can inform their contribution to water security objectives. A total of 106 studies were identified and classified into three groups: forest-based interventions, wetlands, and water harvesting. The four most frequently assessed hydrological functions were flow regulation, water retention, groundwater recharge, and soil erosion control. The evidence was unevenly distributed geographically, with studies concentrated in a limited number of countries. Forest-based interventions showed relatively consistent evidence for flow regulation, whereas evidence for groundwater recharge was more variable. Wetland studies reported effects on flow regulation and water retention, but these varied between sites and assessment approaches. Water harvesting interventions, particularly terraces and infiltration trenches, were frequently linked with runoff reduction and soil erosion control. However, their evidence base was predominantly local in scale and less extensive for several hydrological functions. The reported effect ranges varied within the NbS groups, highlighting the context-dependent nature of their performance and limiting the possibility of direct comparisons between cases. Overall, the review identified recurrent hydrological functions and conditioning factors relevant to mountain NbS, while highlighting important gaps in baseline conditions, methodological assessment, and spatial coverage. papers.title: The rise and fall of a volcanic plateau: Landscape evolution at the fringes of the former Patagonian Ice Sheet, Meseta Chile Chico, central Patagonian Andes
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Understanding Earth‐surface processes along the fringes of large ice sheets is integral to deciphering cold‐region environmental variability and anticipating slope instability under climate change. We investigate the Meseta Chile Chico, a volcanic plateau in the central Patagonian Andes, located at the eastern margin of the former Patagonian Ice Sheet. Here, glacier retreat patterns are well‐constrained, while the influence of periglacial, paraglacial, and postglacial processes is not. We employ geomorphological mapping integrated with geological and palaeoclimate reconstructions to provide a spatio‐temporal model of landscape evolution. Enhanced erosion since the late Pliocene, caused by differential tectonic uplift and glacial isostatic rebound, produced the rugged morphology that characterizes the Meseta Chile Chico. During the Last Glacial Maximum, glaciers occupied surrounding valleys, while the surface of the plateau was reshaped by long‐lasting periglacial freeze‐thaw cycles and nivation. Postglacial landscape adjustment included intensified landslide activity along the edges of the plateau (linked to paraglacial de‐buttressing at its bordering valleys) and regional base‐level changes. During the Holocene, flow‐type landslides became increasingly controlled by climatic variability. The geomorphology of the Meseta Chile Chico reflects an interplay between inherited geology, (de)glaciation, and climate, highlighting the importance of an interdisciplinary approach for understanding recent landscape dynamics in deglaciating mountain regions.

papers.title: Largely Automated Regional Screening of Candidate Active-Slope Units Integrating InSAR and Topographic Constraints
papers.summary: Landslides are among the most serious geohazards worldwide, and accurately identifying their locations is a prerequisite for effective risk prevention and mitigation. However, regional-scale screening of candidate active-slope units from InSAR observations is still hindered by subjective manual interpretation, inconsistent deformation-rate thresholds, and insufficient topographic constraints. To address these limitations, this study proposes a largely automated terrain-constrained framework for candidate active-slope screening by integrating InSAR observations, slope units, and screening based on slope-unit bootstrap intervals and a regional two-standard-deviation background envelope. First, surface deformation rates are derived from InSAR measurements and post-processed to reduce the influence of identifiable artifacts before slope-unit analysis. Then, a clustering-based method is introduced to delineate topographically constrained slope units in alpine canyon regions, whose visual terrain correspondence is examined qualitatively using terrain information and optical imagery. Next, rather than applying a fixed site-specific deformation-rate cutoff in mm/yr, data-dependent bootstrap confidence-interval comparisons are used to determine whether the deformation interval of each slope unit extends beyond the regional deformation-background interval, thereby enabling rule-based screening of candidate active-slope units. This confidence-interval screening rule provides a quantitative criterion for regional screening but requires further calibration across additional geomorphic and deformation settings. Finally, the proposed method is applied to two landslide-prone regions in western China, located in sections of the Upper Yellow River and Upper Jinsha River, where final inventories containing 92 and 25 candidate active-slope units are produced, respectively. These polygons are geomorphologically constrained candidate active-slope units produced for regional screening and

papers.title: Finite Element Greenfield Modelling for building damage assessment under groundwater-induced slope movements
papers.summary: This study presents a numerical investigation of ground movements induced by groundwater rise in slopes using a plane strain finite element model with a Mohr–Coulomb constitutive law under drained, steady-state seepage conditions. The main methodological contribution is the definition of a Greenfield Slope Analysis framework, which adapts the Limiting Tensile Strain Method (LTSM) to assess potential damage in shallow-founded buildings affected by slow-moving landslides. Finite element analyses are used to evaluate displacement and strain fields across the slope from which maximum tensile strains are derived, together with the corresponding changes in slope stability. Groundwater rise leads to progressive increase in ground displacements, whereas the spatial distribution of strain is primarily controlled by slope kinematics. For the selected idealised slopes with a layer of uniform thickness, the central portion shows predominantly translational behaviour, while rotation-like components develop near the crest and toe. The crest is mainly associated with tensile horizontal strains, whereas the toe is mainly associated with compressive horizontal strains, resulting in different damage potential depending on the adopted structural idealisation. Sensitivity and parametric analyses indicate that normalised slope-parallel displacement may be used as a proxy for greenfield deformation levels, supporting preliminary damage assessment and interpretation of in-situ monitoring data.

papers.title: Initial failure morphology of shallow loess containing millimeter-scale cracks: Insights from CT 3d imaging
papers.summary: Frequent shallow loess slope failures in loess regions pose significant threats to both linear infrastructure and local communities. Millimeter-scale initial cracks induced by water, temperature, and weathering are key factors controlling such loess failures. Early diagnosis and prevention remain challenging, largely because the disaster chain triggered by millimeter-scale initial cracks is not fully understood, and the early failure behavior of these cracks is poorly characterized. In this study, laboratory experiments were conducted on loess specimens containing artificial millimeter-scale initial cracks to simulate natural cracks. Uniaxial compression tests combined with CT scanning were performed on specimens with initial cracks of varying characteristics. Three-dimensional structural models of the specimens at initial failure were reconstructed using machine learning methods, and the morphology and structural characteristics of the cracks were analyzed qualitatively and quantitatively. The test results show that the cracks generated in the initial failure state mainly involve wing cracks and extension cracks from the initial crack edges as well as wing cracks extending from both sides, initial cracks of varying characteristics produce different types of secondary cracks. Compared to intact specimens, samples with shallow, 45°-inclined, or shallow-surface compound cracks reached initial failure at substantially lower axial stresses-reduced by 78%, 65%, and 81%, respectively. This reduction is attributed to the development of larger-volume failure cracks in specimens with initial cracks. The distribution, inclination, and combination of millimeter-scale initial cracks exacerbate initial failure.
