Tracing sources and pathways of micro-organic contaminants in a complex peri-urban floodplain aquifer
papers.summary: Peri-urban floodplains include a diverse range of potential contaminant sources and complex surface water-groundwater interactions which control the transport of emerging contaminants in underlying groundwater systems. The impact of an unlined legacy landfill located within the floodplain of the River Thames in southern United Kingdom is assessed with two downgradient multi-depth piezometer transects, and results compared with a control piezometer site previously shown to be unaffected by the landfill leachate plume. Groundwater samples collected from two monitoring rounds in 2017 and 2018 from a network of sites showed the landfill to be a heterogeneous source of contaminants. Over 580 micro-organics (MO) including pharmaceuticals, pesticides, lifestyle products, surfactants and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) were screened in groundwater and surface water using an semi-quantitative LCMS screen. Use of sucralose (an artificial sweetener) post-dates the closure of the landfill. Sucralose found within the landfill plume, together with contaminants found within the control site, suggests a more recent source of contamination also contributes to groundwater contamination within the floodplain. As these samples do not match the fingerprint of the River Thames, it is proposed that the additional contaminant source could be infiltration from either a canal or train wastewater discharge upgradient of the landfill. Spatial variation shows contaminant attenuation down gradient of the landfill with higher concentrations found in the deeper part of the alluvial gravel aquifer system possibly due to local recharge diluting shallow groundwater. Although closed 40 years prior to this study, groundwater sampling has demonstrated that the landfill continues to be a source of persistent, mobile contaminants.

papers.title: Flood simulation and early warning in the XiHanShui River Basin using HEC-HMS
papers.summary: The Xihan River basin is located in the southern part of Gansu Province, where flood disasters occur frequently in summer and autumn, which easily pose significant risks to human life. In order to improve the accuracy of flood disaster predictions and early warnings, a flood model suitable for this region was constructed based on the HEC-HMS (Hydrologic Engineering Center's-hydrologic modeling system) model and used to determine the critical areal rainfall for flood disasters. Calibration of this model was performed using data of four flood events from May to October between 2020 and 2021, reserving data of two additional flood events for model validation. Using the calibrated HEC-HMS model, the critical areal rainfall was determined for the Pingluo and Tanjiaba hydrological stations in the basin through the model testing method. The results indicate that: (1) The stable infiltration rate of the XiHanShui River Basin was between 0.06 and 0.10 mm/h, with runoff concentration times primarily varying from 22.5 to 24.1 hours, a direct runoff storage coefficient was 0.2 hours, and a base flow index decay constant seted at 0.03 hours. (2) During the calibration and validation periods, the average peak flow relative error was 7.56%, the average runoff volume relative error was 14.76%, the average peak occurrence time difference was -0.5 hours, and the Nash efficiency coefficient was 0.769. (3) The warning areal rainfall for the Pingluo and Tanjiaba hydrological stations were 108.1mm and 128.5mm, and the guaranteed areal rainfall were 230.8mm and 184.6mm. The HEC-HMS model demonstrated high applicability and accuracy in simulating flood events in the XiHanShui River Basin, providing technical support for hydrological research and operational applications in the region.

papers.title: Surface-Groundwater Interactions and Climate Change Impacts : An Integrated Approach using HydroGeoSphere Model
papers.summary: Hydrological connectivity between surface water and groundwater supports the resilience of headwater stream networks, yet this connectivity is increasingly threatened by climate-driven shifts in water availability. This cumulative thesis investigates how environmental change alters surface–groundwater exchange, combining fully integrated numerical modelling with field-based tracer evidence and an innovative data-driven approach. The core study area is the 19.2 km2 forested Große Ohe catchment in the Bavarian Forest (Germany), whose steep, wetland-fringed headwaters typify many Central European mountain basins; a complementary coastal application extends the analysis to tidally forced systems. A catchment-scale HydroGeoSphere model was calibrated against observed discharge and then forced with ensembles of RCP-based climate projections. The simulations revealed a pronounced drying trajectory. Mean annual precipitation was projected to decline by 10–20 %, while evapotranspiration remained nearly unchanged, pushing the water balance into persistent deficit. By the late twenty-first century under RCP 8.5, annual deficits increased roughly seven-fold relative to the historical baseline, driving mean streamflow down by up to 34 % and summer baseflow by ~50 %. Falling groundwater heads eroded the hydraulic support that sustains perennial flow: modelled groundwater inputs to upstream reaches contracted by as much as 88 %, and during prolonged dry spells roughly 200 m of the upper channel fell dry, fragmenting the stream network. Thus, even in a humid temperate setting, modest reductions in recharge can trigger a step change from gaining to losing or intermittent conditions. To examine present-day groundwater influence and its spatial variability, longitudinal surveys of dissolved radon-222 (222Rn) were performed at twelve sites along the headwater tributary on 12 June 2018, 27 September 2018 and 12 June 2019. Measured activities ranged from 83 to 2,888 Bq m-3, with repeated

papers.title: Design of a decision platform that focuses on long-term resilience while navigating through environmental shocks
Hydrological decoupling of groundwater from natural climatic forcing in a heavily managed megacity
papers.summary: Introduction Groundwater recharge is traditionally understood to be primarily controlled by precipitation and other climatic processes. However, intensive anthropogenic water management and urbanization may weaken this relationship in megacities. This study investigates hydrological decoupling at the municipal scale in Beijing, China, and quantifies the relative contributions of anthropogenic and climatic drivers to groundwater dynamics. Methods We analyzed 19 years of multisource hydroclimatic data using nonparametric trend analyses, antecedent-window correlation analyses, and hierarchical multiple regression. Spatial analyses were conducted to examine the potential effects of impervious surfaces and managed vegetation on natural groundwater recharge. Future drought risks and groundwater trends were also assessed under the SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 climate scenarios for 2024–2100. Results Annual precipitation showed no statistically significant correlation with groundwater depth (Spearman’s ρ = 0.04, p = 0.624), and no significant delayed associations were identified across antecedent climatic windows of 1–12 months. Hierarchical regression attributed 60.0% of the variance in groundwater depth to anthropogenic drivers, represented by total water supply, compared with 35.6% attributed to natural climatic forcing. Spatial analyses further indicated that dense impervious surfaces and managed vegetation may constrain natural recharge and weaken the influence of meteorological variability on groundwater dynamics. Both future climate scenarios indicated substantial drought risk, while historical evidence suggested that groundwater trajectories would remain strongly influenced by active water management. Discussion The findings indicate that anthropogenic water management can become a dominant control on urban groundwater dynamics, potentially outweighing the influence of climatic variability. This hydrological decoupling challenges conventional assumptions about precipitatio

papers.title: Reviews and syntheses: Threshold shifts in riparian plant water sources along hydrological gradients
papers.summary: Abstract. The hydrological connection between riparian plants and the river underpins riparian ecosystem functioning and informs ecological water delivery and buffer-zone delineation, yet isotope evidence remains scattered across case studies. From a library of 131 stable hydrogen and oxygen isotope (δ²H, δ¹⁸O) water-source studies, we selected 25 studies with an explicit gradient design and re-analysed their data in a standardised form, 11 distance-calibrated transects (41 sites), three time series (158 records) and one water-uptake-depth sequence (43 records). Distance to channel, depth to water table and flow permanence were unified on a single "hydrological connectivity" axis to test for comparable thresholds in water-source switching. In arid and semi-arid regions plant water sources switch abruptly along the distance gradient, and the transition zone in which the stable-water fraction (deep soil water plus groundwater) crosses 50 % consistently falls at 50–400 m from the channel (shrubs 50–100 m and trees 100–400 m in hyper-arid regions, 50–200 m in semi-arid regions). In humid regions no such switch occurs; the river-water signal attenuates over metre-to-hectometre distances, with the attenuation scale increasing with aridity. Recharge mode determines the form of the gradient: channel-recharged systems produce a switch, precipitation-recharged systems attenuation. Life form shifts transition-zone position through rooting depth, and woody species show greater seasonal plasticity than herbs. Distance to channel is itself only a proxy for connectivity, since groundwater contribution increases with distance in a channel-recharge system but decreases with distance in a reservoir-recharge system. We propose defining the functional width of a riparian zone by the outer edge of the transition zone (400–1000 m for trees in arid inland rivers, 100–200 m in semi-humid rivers) and replacing a single target water level with a zoned combination of depth and fluctuation, to

papers.title: Study on the dynamic evolution and driving mechanisms of groundwater in the Northeastern Margin of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, China
papers.summary: Groundwater serves as a critical water source for domestic, industrial, and ecological security in valley-type cities across the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, China. Under the combined pressures of climate change and urbanization, the evolution of regional groundwater systems has become increasingly complex. Taking Xining, a representative valley-type city on the northeastern margin of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, as the study area, this study systematically analyzes the dynamic evolution characteristics and driving mechanisms of groundwater based on groundwater depth data from 126 monitoring wells (1980–2025) and multi-source datasets including precipitation, evaporation, temperature, surface runoff, population, economy, land use, and groundwater extraction. By integrating the Mann–Kendall (M–K) test, Grey Relational Analysis (GRA), and Principal Component Regression (PCR), this study reveals the following findings: From 1980 to 2025, the groundwater depth in Xining increased from 10.7 m to 16.2 m before retreating to 13.5 m, undergoing four distinct phases: continuous decline, rapid rebound, dynamic stability, and slow recovery. Concurrently, precipitation and surface runoff exhibited increasing trends at rates of 1.61 mm/a and 0.06 m³/s, respectively, while evaporation decreased at a rate of 11.52 mm/a and temperature showed a slight decline of 0.007 °C/a. Groundwater extraction rose from 0.32 × 10⁸ m³/a to a peak of 2.30 × 10⁸ m³/a before dropping to 1.18 × 10⁸ m³/a. GRA identified groundwater extraction, precipitation, surface runoff, and population as the factors most closely associated with groundwater-depth variation, with relational degrees of 0.862, 0.816, 0.736, and 0.709, respectively. PCR further showed that anthropogenic and natural factors accounted for 59.1% and 40.9% of the relative contribution, respectively. These results indicate that anthropogenic factors provided a greater explanatory contribution to the long-term evolution of groundwater depth during t

papers.title: Regional-scale assessment of climate change impacts on land use–specific hydrological processes in the Geum River Basin, South Korea
papers.summary: Study region Geum River Basin, South Korea, East Asia Study focus Climate change is expected to substantially modify hydrological processes: however, the mechanisms underlying these changes remain highly dependent on regional characteristics and land use patterns. In this study, we provide a regional-scale assessment of the effects of climate change on land use specifics hydrological processes in the Geum River Basin, South Korea, which is a key water-supply region characterized by rapid urbanization and a mixture of agricultural– and forested landscapes. New hydrological insights for the region Climate change is intensifying hydrological variability across the Geum River Basin, with fast-response components such as surface runoff generally increasing. However, slow-response components, particularly groundwater recharge and baseflow, are projected to decline. Runoff sensitivities to precipitation and temperature exhibit three distinct response patterns corresponding to urban land, agricultural land, and forestland–grassland, demonstrating that climate drivers propagate through hydrological processes in land use–specific ways. Although projected increases in precipitation enhance meteorological resilience, they do not necessarily translate into improved hydrological water availability, especially in highly urbanized sub-basins. These findings highlight the importance of regionally tailored adaptation strategies. For the Geum River Basin, expanding storage capacity, conserving permeable and vegetated surfaces, and improving seasonal water allocation are identified as priority measures for sustaining water and ecosystem resilience under future climate conditions.

papers.title: Improved permafrost soil representation in a dynamic global vegetation model enhances simulations of carbon dynamics and vegetation structure in boreal forests of Northeast China
papers.summary: Abstract. Boreal forests constitute a major component of the global terrestrial carbon sink, yet how climate-driven permafrost degradation alters their ecosystem carbon dynamics remains poorly constrained. Despite their importance, the persistence of this carbon sink remains highly uncertain, partly due to limitations in Earth system model projections of future carbon dynamics in permafrost-affected regions. Here, we improve the soil module of the LPJ-GUESS model by implementing a deep soil profile (3 m) with refined vertical discretization (30 layers) and explicit ice-impedance effects. The enhanced model (LPJ-GUESS-Cryo) is then used to simulate carbon and hydrothermal dynamics in the climate-sensitive boreal forests of Northeast China. Model evaluation shows that LPJ-GUESS-Cryo substantially improves the simulation of soil hydrothermal dynamics relative to the default configuration. The correlation coefficient for deep soil temperature (1 m) increases from 0.818 to 0.894, while the systematic overestimation of soil water content is effectively corrected, with the bias at 1 m reduced from 0.321 to -0.006. These process-level improvements lead to a more realistic simulation of vegetation composition. The dominance of needleleaf forests is corrected from near-complete saturation to 24.1 %, consistent with observed vegetation patterns. Consequently, biases in carbon estimates are reduced, with simulated net primary productivity decreasing from 583.5 to 560.1 g C m-2 yr-1 and aboveground biomass from 112.9 to 99.0 t ha-1, resulting in better agreement with estimates from satellite-based observations. Model sensitivity analysis indicates that vegetation composition is highly sensitive to changes in soil hydrothermal conditions relative to the control simulation. Pronounced shifts in vegetation composition occur when soil temperature increases exceed 0.6 °C and soil water deficits exceed 0.6 m3 m-3 compared to the default model configuration. Overall, this study highlig

papers.title: Effects of moss restoration on topsoil water dynamics in a temperate vineyard
papers.summary: Abstract. Climate change is intensifying pressure on vineyard soil and water management, particularly under-vine, where vegetation is commonly suppressed to minimize competition with grapevines. Bryophytes represent a promising but little-tested alternative to bare soil or cover crops. We evaluated moss restoration as an under-vine ground cover in a temperate, rainfed vineyard in southwestern Germany, comparing it with bare soil and cover crop (grass) over a 22-month field experiment. Continuous topsoil moisture measurements using time-domain transmission sensors were used to analyse the initial response time (the time between the onset of precipitation and the first increase in topsoil moisture) and the peak response time (the time between the onset of precipitation and the maximum topsoil moisture). We additionally quantified mean topsoil moisture and drying rates and monitored treatment development during and after maintenance. Moss restoration did not significantly delay topsoil moisture response times following precipitation compared to grass or bare soil. Initial response times followed the pattern grass > moss > bare soil; differences between treatments were most pronounced under light and moderate precipitation and declined with increasing intensity, with moss and bare soil converging under heavy events. Peak response times followed a similar pattern (grass > moss ≈ bare soil), with significant differences restricted to light and heavy precipitation events: grass exhibited longer peak response times than bare soil under light rainfall and longer times than both bare soil and moss under heavy rainfall. Mean topsoil moisture did not differ significantly among treatments, whereas drying rates were higher under moss and bare soil than under grass. Moss plots initially suppressed grass establishment and consistently exhibited the lowest variability in topsoil moisture response, although vegetation cover and functional differences between treatments gradually conv

papers.title: Extreme precipitation rapidly recharges desiccated deep soil and restores deep root water uptake in a rainfed apple orchard: Implications for water management in deep-rooted agroecosystems
papers.summary: Deep soil water is a critical resource for deep-rooted tree crops in water-limited regions, yet progressive desiccation of deep layers under rainfed plantations may erode the long-term drought resilience of these systems and threaten their productivity. However, the extent to which extreme rainfall events can recharge desiccated deep soil and restore deep root water uptake remains poorly quantified. To address this gap, we used the 2021 extreme wet year, when annual precipitation reached 920 mm—approximately 1.6 times the long-term mean—as a natural experiment in a mature rainfed apple orchard on the Loess Plateau of China. We compared soil water dynamics down to 20 m, tree transpiration, and stable-isotope-based water source partitioning in 2017 and 2023, representing conditions before and after the extreme wet year, to quantify how extreme precipitation altered deep soil water reserves and plant water use. Extreme precipitation rapidly replenished the 3–10 m soil layer, increasing water storage by about 350 mm. The infiltration rate reached 5 m yr⁻1—approximately 25 times faster than previously reported piston flow rates, indicating preferential-flow-dominated deep recharge. This replenishment reduced transpiration stress: despite a lower leaf area index in 2023 than in 2017, actual transpiration increased from 213 to 232 mm, and the Ta/Tp ratio rose from 0.57 ± 0.24 to 0.78 ± 0.31. In addition, the contribution of soil water from 3–10 m depth to transpiration increased from 50 ± 12% in 2017 to 62 ± 12% in 2023, indicating a shift in water uptake from shallow to deeper soil layers. These findings demonstrate that episodic extreme precipitation can reverse deep soil desiccation in deep-rooted rainfed orchards, and provide a quantitative basis for rainwater-harvesting and infiltration-enhancing strategies that convert such events into a hydraulic buffer against drought in water-limited agricultural regions under a changing climate.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal variations of carbon-water-hydraulic risk for Pinus tabuliformis Carrière Plantations on the Loess Plateau under future climate change
papers.summary: Abstract. As a native perennial tree, Pinus tabuliformis L. (PT) has been widely planted on the Chinese Loess Plateau for ecological restoration. However, climate change impacts on water resources will poses a new challenge for sustainability of restored ecosystems. To clarify the plantations carbon sequestration and water consumption, as well as their underlying physiological mechanisms, this study coupled the integrated BBGC-Sperry model with CMIP6 meteorological data under SSP126, SSP245, and SSP585. Daily transpiration, soil water content, and leaf water potential, along with multi-site total growing-season transpiration and aboveground biomass data, were used to validate the BBGC-Sperry model. The validated model simulated the dynamics of NPP, actual evapotranspiration (ET) and annual average percentage loss of whole-plant hydraulic conductivity (APLK) for PT plantations at 130 meteorological stations on the Loess Plateau. We integrated a “carbon-water-hydraulic risk index” (CWHRI) based on NPP, ET, and drought-induced mortality risk probability (DMRP) to assess ecosystem sustainability. These simulations covered the baseline period (2000–2024) and three future periods (2025–2049, NFP; 2050–2074, MFP; and 2075–2099, FFP). The results indicate that the mean NPP will decrease by 4 %–27 % except in the FFP under the SSP585 while the mean ET and APLK will increase by 0.05 %–61 % and 13 %–84 %, respectively. The CWHRI will decline by 23 %–44 %, driven directly by NPP and indirectly by water-related environmental factors. The spatial dynamics of CWHRI will decline from southeast to northwest. These findings indicate the rising DMRP of PT plantations will threaten the sustainability of restored ecosystems on the Loess Plateau in the future.

papers.title: Impacts of post-fire straw mulching on plant diversity dynamics and mid-term persistence of introduced weed species in a Mediterranean chronosequence
papers.summary: Post-fire straw mulching is widely used to reduce soil erosion and facilitate vegetation recovery in fire-affected ecosystems. However, straw mulch may introduce agricultural weedy species, raising concerns about their persistence and potential effects on post-fire plant community assembly. This study evaluated the medium-term ecological implications of straw mulch application using a post-fire chronosequence in semi-arid Mediterranean ecosystems of southeastern Spain. Vegetation was surveyed in 54 plots (27 mulched and 27 untreated) distributed across sites representing 1, 2 and 6 years after fire (YAF). Species richness, diversity, composition and the abundance of agricultural weedy species were analysed to assess treatment effects across the chronosequence. Straw mulching increased species richness and diversity during the early post-fire stages, through the introduction of agricultural weedy species. Community composition differed significantly among post-fire stages and between treatments, although post-fire stage explained a substantially larger proportion of the variation than mulching treatment. The abundance of agricultural weedy species declined markedly along the chronosequence, and these species showed very low abundance at the site representing 6 YAF. Plant communities in mulched and untreated plots became more similar at the latest stage represented in the chronosequence. Overall, the results suggest that straw mulching can temporarily enhance plant diversity during early post-fire recovery without evidence of negative medium-term effects on vegetation recovery under the environmental conditions evaluated in this study. These findings support the use of straw mulching as a post-fire restoration measure in semi-arid Mediterranean ecosystems while highlighting the importance of considering straw provenance when assessing early community responses.

papers.title: Ecohydrological coupling and episodic hydrological connectivity in the Edwards Plateau
papers.summary: Abstract. In semiarid karst systems, the hydrologic budget is regulated by strong interactions among the water fluxes of precipitation, soil water dynamics, evapotranspiration, runoff, and groundwater recharge. In this study, we evaluated the temporal coupling among these fluxes in the Edwards Plateau Balcones Fault Zone (Texas, USA) using five years (2021–2025) of daily observations of precipitation (P), soil water content (SWC), evapotranspiration (ET), runoff (Rf), and groundwater (GW). Soil water content responses to precipitation exhibited threshold-dependent behavior under both dry and wet antecedent conditions, with breakpoints at 66.9 and 32.6 mm, respectively. Evapotranspiration dynamics were jointly controlled by SWC and temperature, with strong limitations under dry soil conditions and maximum ET values occurring only under warm and wet conditions. In contrast, Rf and GW responses were highly episodic and associated with the relatively rare large precipitation events. Although both fluxes increased rapidly following rainfall inputs, Rf responses were short-lived whereas GW responses persisted for several weeks to months. Groundwater recharge exhibited a clear threshold response, occurring only after precipitation events greater than 78 mm and never following events smaller than 62 mm. On the basis of these findings, we have developed a conceptual model for semiarid karst ecosystems whereby hydrological connectivity is activated during short-lived windows created only when precipitation pulses exceed both atmospheric demand and internal storage thresholds.

papers.title: Coupled Effects of Burial Depth and Surface Double Cracks on the Uplift Bearing Capacity of Strip Anchor Plates in Red Clay
papers.summary: Prolonged drought can induce shrinkage cracking in near-surface clay foundations, leaving persistent defects that may affect the uplift safety of underground structures before subsequent rainfall events. This study investigates how burial depth regulates the influence of two pre-existing surface cracks on the uplift bearing capacity and failure mechanism of a horizontal strip anchor plate in red clay. A two-dimensional plane-strain model was established in Optum G2 and validated against laboratory pull-out tests under crack-free conditions. Two burial-depth ratios, H/B = 3 and 8, were examined, and 360 cases were generated by varying normalized crack depth (h/B = 0.25–3), spacing (s/B = 0.25–3), and horizontal offset (d/B = 0–6). Under shallow burial, cracks readily intersect the potential sliding zone and the maximum capacity reduction reaches 81.6%, with pronounced transitions around s/B = 1 and d/B = 1. Under deep burial, the principal failure surface remains predominantly a deep elliptical arc and capacity reduction is generally below 15%. Burial depth therefore controls the spatial overlap between the environmentally damaged zone and the anchor-bearing zone. The results provide a mechanical basis for post-drought crack inspection, uplift-safety reassessment, and burial-depth selection. Hydraulic infiltration, suction, moisture evolution, and rainfall intensity are outside the present model.

papers.title: Modelling the spatial dynamics of flood inundation in Bayelsa State, Nigeria, using remote sensing and machine learning techniques
papers.summary: Abstract Flooding is a persistent environmental challenge in Bayelsa State, Nigeria, driven by low-lying terrain, high rainfall, and inadequate drainage systems. This study evaluates flood susceptibility in the Lower Niger Basin using a geospatial modelling approach. Ten flood-conditioning factors; rainfall, drainage density, slope, elevation, soil texture, land use/land cover (LULC), Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), and proximity to rivers were integrated within a Random Forest (RF) framework. Spatial datasets were processed using ArcGIS and Google Earth Engine, and the model was trained with historical flood and non-flood locations to produce a high-resolution susceptibility map. Results indicate that areas receiving 2500 to 3199 mm of annual rainfall, particularly Southern Ijaw, Ekeremor, and Brass, exhibit the highest flood susceptibility. Over 82% of the region is characterized by low slopes (0 to 3°) and elevations ranging from 16 to 41 m, increasing flood vulnerability. High drainage density zones (up to 0.677 km/km²) contribute to flash flooding, while clay and sandy clay loam soils (covering > 60% of the area) reduce infiltration and enhance runoff. Built-up areas and regions with NDVI < 0.1 are also associated with higher flood risk. The RF model achieved an accuracy of 91%, with high-risk zones predominantly located within 1 km of major rivers. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of integrating machine learning with geospatial analysis for flood susceptibility mapping in data-scarce, low-lying environments. The resulting map provides a reliable decision-support tool for flood risk management, land-use planning, and targeted mitigation strategies in Bayelsa State.

papers.title: Practical Insights on the Hydrological Response of Simulated Soil-Layered Low Impact Development (LID) Practices in Brazilian Tropical Regions
authors: Frederico Carlos Martins de Menezes Filho
papers.summary: Previous studies regarding Low Impact Development (LID) practices used physical and hydraulic soil layer properties recommended by the literature for temperate climates in tropical climate locations; however, the effect of these properties on LID practices behaviour has still been unexplored. The study’s objective was to determine by modelling the effect of adopting LID practices soil layer properties according to recommendations for temperate climate in relation to those of two tropical soils determined in laboratory, and to evaluate a practical and low-cost way to obtain such properties, by using a pedotransfer function. The values of the soil’s physical and hydraulic properties influenced the hydrological response of LID practices. The adoption of values recommended by the literature should be carefully evaluated, since these may lead to significantly different results in relation to those that would be obtained considering the soils of the implementation area, especially those located in a different climate zone, such as tropical zone. LID practices that have drainage layer connected to an overflow, such as the bioretention cell, may compromise the detention and infiltration of the runoff, even in soils that have physical and hydraulic properties that would provide greater infiltration.

papers.title: Rainfall infiltration-induced vertical differentiation of pore structure and permeability in mine tailings: a throat-dominated mechanism
papers.source: International Journal of Mining Reclamation and Environment
papers.summary: Seepage-induced particle migration in tailings alters pore structures, risking dam stability. This study quantitatively assesses vertical pore structure differentiation during sustained rainfall infiltration using micro-CT and pore network modelling (PNM). Results show that total porosity varies by 5%, while connected porosity declines by nearly 20%. Surface layers develop high-connectivity networks via throat expansion, while deep-layer networks degrade due to pore isolation and particle depletion. PNM simulations validate that throat radius governs permeability evolution, showing significantly higher sensitivity than pore radius, consistent with Hagen-Poiseuille law. This reveals heterogeneous permeability distributions, indicating that characterising pore network topology is essential for understanding tailings seepage behaviour.

papers.title: Land use dynamics and hydro-climatic variability to hydrological responses in Tawa River Basin, central India
papers.summary: Quantifying hydrological responses of river basins to combined hydro-climatic variability and land use/land cover (LULC) change (1999–2019) is fundamental to sustainable water resource management in regions experiencing intensifying anthropogenic pressures. This study investigates how climatic variability and land-use dynamics drive hydrological change in the Tawa River Basin, a strategically important tributary of the Narmada River in central India, whose hydrological behaviour underpins regional agricultural productivity, ecosystem functioning, and water supply security. The primary objective is to detect, attribute, and quantify shifts in surface runoff generation, streamflow variability, and water balance partitioning driven by interacting climatic and land-use forcing. Long-term hydro-climatic data were analysed using ordinary least squares regression, coefficient of variation, standardized anomaly, Mann–Kendall trend detection, and Sen’s slope estimation. Basin rainfall exhibits moderate inter-annual variability (CV ≈ 19.7%) with a slight increasing trend, implying potential augmentation of surface runoff and flood frequency. Temperature displays a consistent warming trend of 0.012 °C per year (≈0.24 °C per decade), with persistently positive anomalies characterising the post-2009 period signalling increased evapotranspiration demand, reduced base flow, and altered seasonal streamflow regimes. Concurrently, LULC transitions particularly expansion of agricultural and built-up areas at the expense of natural vegetation have reduced infiltration capacity and amplified direct runoff response. An attribution framework disaggregated observed hydrological change into climatically driven and land-use-driven components, demonstrating that both exert significant and distinguishable influences on the basin’s hydrological regime. These findings carry direct implications for reservoir inflow estimation, flood risk assessment, and long-term water resource planning across th

papers.title: Integrated Geological Mineralogical and Geophysical Characterisation of the Efon Alaaye Basement Terrain in Southwestern Nigeria for Slope Stability and Infrastructure Development
papers.summary: Abstract Efon Alaaye, Ekiti State in southwestern Nigeria, is located within the Precambrian Basement Complex with features of rugged topography, heterogeneous crystalline rocks with variable weathering profiles. This study combines geological mapping, structural measurements, slope assessment, natural-electric-field/electromagnetic reconnaissance survey, X-ray fluorescence (XRF) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to define the geology of the materials and its implications for slope stability, groundwater occurrence and infrastructure development. Based on field observations granite, quartzite, schist, laterite and minor pegmatite were picked out; and the discontinuities were mainly NW-SE and NE-SW. Five slope traverses were recorded on an inclination range of 25–42°, the maximum slope inclination is 42° and this slope inclination is the greatest recon level concern due to steepness, fracturing and erosion susceptibility. The results of XRF analyses are extremely silica-rich, from 97.12 to 98.44 wt. % SiO₂, with the other major oxides present at very low levels. The diffractograms shown here indicate that quartz reflections are significant in all three samples. Reconnaissance geophysical interpretation delineates surficial material, clayey/weathered horizons, partly fractured basement and deeper basement crystalline, it can be seen that engineering behaviour is controlled by combined effects of lithology, discontinuity geometry, weathering, groundwater and slope morphology. Steep, fractured, deeply weathered and seepage prone areas should be assessed geotechnically and properly drained, and development should be avoided on these areas.Gently sloping ground with a good drainage capacity underlain by verified competent material is preferable for development, while the steep, fractured, deeply weathered and seepage prone areas require detailed geotechnical assessment and drainage control.

papers.title: Analysis of Slope Stability of Spoil Grounds Under the Coupling Effect of Reservoir Water Level Rise and Rainfall Infiltration
papers.summary: To investigate the seepage evolution and instability mechanism of gully-type spoil ground slopes under the coupled effect of reservoir water level rise and rainfall infiltration, a typical second-grade gully-type spoil ground of the Jinghe Dongzhuang Water Conservancy Hub was selected as the case study. The SEEP/W and SLOPE/W modules of GeoStudio were employed to perform coupled numerical simulations of unsaturated seepage and slope stability. The reservoir water level was set to rise from 90 m to 120 m at a rate of 1.2 m/d, combined with six continuous rainfall intensities (duration: 25 days) of 20, 40, 80, 120, 160, and 200 mm/d. Reference scenarios involving only reservoir water level rise and only rainfall infiltration were additionally considered. The zoning response characteristics of pore water pressure at the slope front and rear were analyzed, and the individual contributions and coupled effect of rainfall and reservoir water level were quantitatively distinguished using a contribution decomposition method. The results indicate that the pore water pressure at the slope front is mainly governed by reservoir water level rise, whereas the pore water pressure at the slope rear is highly sensitive to rainfall infiltration. As the rainfall intensity increases from 20 mm/d to 200 mm/d, the factor of safety under the coupled condition decreases from 1.611 to 0.969. Furthermore, the dominant factor of instability evolves with rainfall intensity: the contribution decomposition results show that under higher rainfall intensities (80–200 mm/d), the rainfall-only contribution rate ranges from 43.6% to 57.0%, while, under lower rainfall intensities (20–40 mm/d), reservoir water level rise becomes the dominant factor. Throughout all coupled scenarios, the additional coupling contribution rate ranges from 18.2% to 52.9%, indicating a significant non-additive coupled hazard effect between the two factors. Based on the instability criterion of Fs < 1.0, the critical rainfall

papers.title: Seasonal Assessment of the Physicochemical Quality of Groundwater used for Domestic Purposes at a University Campus in Benin City, Nigeria
papers.summary: The study seasonal assessment of the physicochemical quality of groundwater used for domestic purposes at a university campus in Benin city, Nigeria. A total of 24 water samples were collected during the dry and rainy seasons and analyzed at Martlet Environmental Laboratory. Parameters examined included pH, colour, turbidity, conductivity, total dissolved solids, hardness, chloride, dissolved oxygen, biochemical oxygen demand, calcium, magnesium, zinc, copper and iron. The results indicated that the water was generally clear and free from detectable turbidity. Most parameters, including conductivity, total dissolved solids, hardness, chloride, dissolved oxygen and biochemical oxygen demand, were within WHO, SON and NAFDAC permissible limits. Iron(fe) was detected, while magnesium generally complied with WHO and NAFDAC standards, although some girls' hostel samples exceeded the SON requirement. The major concern was the acidic nature of the groundwater, with pH values ranging from 5.0 to 6.0 during the dry season and PH valves ranging 4.0 to 6.0. Conductivity and zinc concentrations increased during the rainy season, possibly due to the infiltration of human waste into the aquifer. Iron concentrations also exceeded NAFDAC and SON limits during the rainy season. The study concludes that the groundwater requires treatment before consumption, particularly for pH correction. It recommends neutralizer filtration, improved sanitation, proper septic-tank and latrine management, regular cleaning of storage tanks, routine sanitary inspections and further microbiological analysis.

papers.title: Accounting of good agricultural practices in north-western hill agri-food systems
papers.summary: Accounting of Good Agricultural Practices (GAPs) in hill agri-food systems means tracking, quantifying and reporting the financial costs, environmental impacts and compliance premiums of sustainable mountain farming. The GAPs address the main weaknesses of hill agriculture such as water erosion, moisture stress, declining soil fertility and low diversification; and support climate resilience by improving infiltration, reducing runoff and stabilising production under aberrant conditions. Monetary accounting covers two linked benefits i.e. direct farm gains, and the additional value of the ecosystem services that GAPs protect or enhance. Thus, GAPs, raise private income and can also justify payments for ecosystem services, because society benefits from cleaner water, healthier soils, carbon storage and biodiversity.

papers.title: Numerical simulation and monitoring experiment of liquid injection diffusion range in ionic rare earth ores
papers.summary: Abstract Currently, in-situ leaching is the predominant method for extracting ionic rare earth ores. However, this technique still faces persistent challenges such as low resource utilization efficiency and environmental issues including water and soil contamination. Clarifying the diffusion characteristics of the leach liquid is crucial for addressing these problems. Geophysical methods, particularly conductive electrical techniques, have been widely employed to monitor the diffusion range of the leach liquid. Nevertheless, these methods suffer from limitations such as operational complexity, high costs, and poor timeliness. To overcome these drawbacks, this study first utilizes numerical simulation to determine the influence range of liquid injection, and subsequently evaluates the effectiveness of the high-density resistivity method in delineating its diffusion extent. Based on the deep structural characteristics of a rare earth mine in Fujian, China, identified through high-density resistivity method, a suitable site was selected for a comparative experiment. The experiment compared time-lapse resistivity tomography monitoring with seepage numerical simulations of liquid injection faced actual geological model, and the results demonstrated good consistency in the diffusion ranges identified by both methods. Through theoretical analysis and comparative monitoring results, this study proposes that the integrated approach of “detailed deep structure investigation & seepage numerical simulation of liquid injection” can effectively characterize the diffusion behavior of the leach liquor. This provides theoretical support for the precise placement of injection wells and the design of anti-seepage systems in ionic rare earth mining. contributing to improved mineral recovery rates and reduced environmental pollution from liquid injection.

papers.title: Modelling-Based Assessment of Managed Aquifer Recharge: Impacts on Groundwater Quantity and Quality in the Upper Friuli Plain (Italy)
papers.summary: In the Friuli Venezia Giulia (FVG) region of northeastern Italy, declining groundwater levels and changing precipitation patterns have raised concerns about the long-term sustainability of groundwater resources. This study evaluates the potential of Managed Aquifer Recharge (MAR) in the upper Friuli Plain, with a focus on the Sammardenchia site. Surface water and groundwater quality in the study area were characterized through the analysis of inorganic and organic compounds, as well as microbiological indicators. A three-dimensional groundwater flow model was developed to simulate the regional and local site-specific hydrogeological conditions. MAR performance was assessed under different recharge scenarios, including an infiltration pond, a recharge well, and a combined pond-well recharge, based on the existing recharge structures at the site. In addition, solute transport simulations were conducted to analyze the behaviour of faecal indicator bacteria (E. coli), detected in the surface water to be used for MAR. The simulation results show that recharge through both the infiltration pond and the well increased the groundwater levels near the MAR site, with the combined recharge scenario producing the highest simulated rise in groundwater levels (~ 2.68 m) and storage. Microbial transport simulations showed substantial attenuation of E. coli during subsurface transport, particularly under the pond-recharge scenario (> 4 log) due to longer residence times. Overall, the modelling results indicate that MAR can effectively contribute to groundwater storage enhancement and attenuation of microbial contamination in the study area. Combined pond−well recharge shows the greatest potential to increase groundwater storage. Longer travel times help reduce simulated E. coli concentrations in groundwater. Different recharge configurations offer distinct benefits, depending on groundwater management objectives.

papers.title: Distributed bioretention under tropical rainfall and tidal backwater: a SWMM-LID assessment for a catchment in Ho Chi Minh City
papers.source: Journal of Scientific and Technological Innovations
papers.summary: Green infrastructure (GI) is widely promoted for urban flood control, yet the performance figures most often quoted come from temperate cities and are a poor guide for tropical, tide-affected deltas. The aim of this study is to quantify, with a locally-parameterised model, how much a distributed bioretention retrofit can deliver in Ho Chi Minh City (HCMC) and what limits it. In terms of materials and methods, we built a hydrodynamic SWMM model of a real sixteen-conduit, six-kilometre trunk sub-catchment (~48 ha) extracted from the surveyed municipal sewer network of the former District 8, draining to a single outfall on the tidal Kênh Đôi canal; the model was forced with design storms of 15–180 min built from the national-standard intensity–duration–frequency (IDF) relation for HCMC (TCVN 7957:2023, 10-year return period, cross-checked against a peer-reviewed 33-year station IDF), bounded downstream by a measured Phú An spring-tide series, and calibrated against the surveyed street-flood depths of the 6 August 2020 storm (Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) 0.77, RMSE 0.03 m, PBIAS −10%).+ The main results are that bioretention on 5% of the catchment reduced the outfall peak by only 0.6–2.1% for storms of 60 min and longer (41.2% for the short 15-min burst), because the flat, surcharged, tidally-controlled network is capacity-limited; the substantial and robust benefit is instead a reduction in flood (street-ponding) volume of 33% for the 60-min design storm and up to 84.7% for short bursts, together with a 6.4–19% runoff-volume reduction and, over a continuous wet season, a 12.7% volume and 33.9% flooding reduction, while a coincident spring tide raised flooding by 15–56%. In discussion, these findings reframe distributed GI in HCMC as a flood-volume and flood-frequency measure for frequent, short convective storms, to be deployed at several percent of the drained area and integrated with the grey and tidal-control system rather than used as a substitute for it. papers.title: Forest structural mediation of hydrological processes and ecosystem multifunctionality: mechanisms, trade-offs, and adaptive management
papers.source: Frontiers in Forests and Global Change
papers.summary: Forests provide multiple ecosystem services, including water regulation, water supply, soil retention, carbon sequestration, habitat provision, biodiversity conservation, and timber production. These services arise from coupled processes operating across vegetation, litter, soil, and watershed compartments. Changes in climate, land use, forest structure, or management can therefore alter several services simultaneously, but the direction of change depends on the process pathway, environmental context, and scale of assessment. Here, we synthesize advances in the quantitative assessment of interactions between forest hydrological functions and other ecosystem services, emphasizing how environmental drivers and management reorganize forest structure, how structural states alter hydrological partitioning and water-carbon coupling, and how these process changes propagate to ecosystem-service outcomes. We first establish a process-based framework covering canopy interception, throughfall, stemflow, litter interception, infiltration, evapotranspiration, soil-water storage, deep drainage, groundwater recharge, lateral flow, baseflow, and surface runoff. We then evaluate field experiments, watershed observations, process-based and ecosystem-service models, spatial statistics, machine learning, and causal inference, with explicit attention to their assumptions and scale limitations. Quantitative evidence from global thinning syntheses and classical catchment experiments is used to distinguish relatively consistent responses from context-dependent ones. A long-term Korean pine forest-management experiment on Changbai Mountain is included as an illustrative case study: the treatments persisted for 27 years, whereas the hydrological measurements summarized here represent observations made in 2023 rather than a continuous 27-year hydrological time series. papers.title: Combined aeromagnetic, GIS, and remote sensing evaluation of flash-flood susceptibility and groundwater potential in an arid environment: Wadi Marwani, Western Saudi Arabia
papers.summary: Introduction Groundwater is the primary dependable freshwater source in the arid coastal catchments of western Saudi Arabia, where natural recharge is limited and occurs mainly through episodic rainfall and flash‐flood infiltration along wadi systems. This study assesses groundwater potential in the Wadi Marwani basin (≈2,347 km 2 ), a major tributary of the Khulais system southeast of Rabigh, by integrating multi‐source remote sensing, GIS, and aeromagnetic data. Methods Lithology was mapped from Sentinel‐2 imagery using support vector machine (SVM) classification, while structural fabrics were constrained using Sentinel‐1C SAR lineaments and aeromagnetic structural analysis. Terrain attributes (e.g., elevation, slope, drainage and flow indices, topographic wetness, and ruggedness) derived from a 30 m digital elevation model (DEM), together with NDVI, soil moisture, rainfall, and 10 m land‐cover data, characterized the surface conditions that control infiltration and storage. Aeromagnetic data were reduced to the pole, upward continued, and enhanced using the modified Elliott function (MEF) filter and Center for Exploration Targeting (CET) grid analysis. Source Parameter Imaging (SPI) was then applied to estimate relative depth to magnetic basement. Results Surface and magnetic lineaments consistently define a dominant N–S to NNW–SSE trend with subsidiary NW–SE and NE–SW sets that remain coherent at depth, reflecting reactivated Pan–African structures. A magnetically subdued, elongate basement depression along the central wadi axis, widening westwards, coincides with high lineament density and thick Quaternary alluvium, indicating favorable conditions for groundwater accumulation. The integrated groundwater potential map divides the basin into five classes; comparison with existing wells yields an AUC of 0.789, indicating acceptable to good predictive skill. papers.title: SlopeTH
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: SlopeTH is a stand-alone Windows program for two-dimensional slope stability analysis by the limitequilibrium method. It finds the critical circular slip surface and reports the factor of safety (FS) by fivemethods, for dry, saturated and unsaturated soils, reinforced and improved ground, earth dams andslopes under rainfall. Main features Methods: Ordinary (Fellenius), Simplified Bishop, Janbu simplified (with correction factor f0),Spencer and Morgenstern-Price (half-sine), the last two by the general limit equilibrium (GLE)formulation. Geometry: any number of soil layers, polygon material regions (e.g. the clay core of a dam),bedrock (impenetrable) materials, slopes facing left or right, choice of slip direction. Water: phreatic surface or pore-pressure ratio ru; reservoir (ponded) water on the slope face; rapiddrawdown. Unsaturated soils: matric suction by the φb, Khalili or Vanapalli models; soil-water characteristiccurve (SWCC) by van Genuchten, Fredlund-Xing, Brooks-Corey or Gardner; hydraulic conductivityfrom the SWCC. Suction profiles: hydrostatic, constant, steady rainfall/evaporation flux, and transient rainfallinfiltration by the Richards equation, giving FS against time. Ground improvement: geotextiles, geogrids, soil nails and anchors; pile and cement-column rows(piled embankments); improved-ground zones (DCM blocks) with a composite-strength calculator. Loads: surcharges and a pseudo-static seismic coefficient kh. Search: grid of centres × tangent lines with FS contours and automatic refinement. Output: text report, slice-by-slice table, FS-time chart, pore-pressure contours, CSV export andfigures in PNG, PDF or SVG. Units. papers.title: Landslide Susceptibility Assessment of Lixian County, Gansu Province, China Using a Physics‐Integrated Multi‐Task Neural Network
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Landslide susceptibility assessment (LSA) is a critical strategy for disaster prevention and mitigation. However, current machine learning‐based LSA algorithms often exhibit instability under data‐sparse conditions and suffer from a lack of physical interpretability. To address these challenges, this study proposes a physics‐integrated multi‐task neural network (PIMTN). The proposed framework incorporates slope‐stability information derived from the infinite slope model into a multi‐task neural network through an auxiliary learning task. The model simultaneously performs landslide susceptibility classification and learns a physics‐derived diluted probability of failure (DPOF). Through joint optimization, the auxiliary DPOF task influences the shared representation and guides susceptibility prediction towards spatial patterns consistent with physics‐derived slope‐stability information. Comparative experiments demonstrate that the PIMTN outperforms benchmark models (Precision: 0.737, F 1‐Score: 0.754, AUC: 0.817). Furthermore, quantitative analysis confirms the superiority of the proposed model and the effectiveness of knowledge transfer from the physical domain. This framework presents a novel solution for enhancing model interpretability and improving predictive robustness under limited‐inventory conditions.

papers.title: Drought to Flood Abrupt Alternation Events Across Monsoon Region in China: Characteristics, Mechanisms, and Crop Exposure
papers.summary: Abstract Climate change is altering the frequency and intensity of hydroclimatic extremes, increasing the likelihood of drought to flood abrupt alternation (DTFAA) events which creates compound risks. Here, we identify DTFAA events across the monsoon region of China (MRC) during May–September from 1961 to 2023 using the daily Standardized Weighted Average Precipitation index. We identify 3,575 DTFAA events, with most transitions occurring within 1–2 days and a modest maximum in June. Generally, DTFAA frequency and intensity in MRC increase significantly at rates of 0.29 times decade⁻¹ and 0.26 decade⁻¹, respectively, with high frequencies concentrated in the middle and lower Yangtze River Basin, southern coastal China, and parts of North and Southwest China. Dynamically, governed by jet-waveguide interaction, the transition initiates with high-latitude easterly anomalies anchoring upstream blocking and the westward-extending subtropic high priming baroclinicity. Subsequently, the intensified and westward-extending subtropical jet establishes a mid-latitude meridional potential vorticity gradient conduit, routing trapped energy in blocking downstream to drive deep dynamic suction and moisture convergence, unleashing the abrupt flooding. Furthermore, crop exposure is crop-specific heterogeneous: maize and wheat show extensive high-exposure belts, whereas rice exposure is more fragmented; maize exhibits significant increases in both frequency and intensity exposure during 2000–2019. These results demonstrate that DTFAA events in the MRC arise from coordinated large-scale circulation and moisture-transport processes and that their agricultural consequences are strongly crop and region dependent, providing a dynamical and impact-oriented framework for improving monitoring, prediction, and adaptation to rapid hydroclimatic transitions.

papers.title: Management of Stormwater through Green Infrastructure Systems in Coastal Urban Areas: Hydrological Modelling, Compound-Flood Response, and Water-Quality Performance
papers.source: AlQalam Journal of Medical and Applied Sciences
papers.summary: In seven different GI scenarios, a representative 120 ha coastal urban drainage catchment, typical of Alexandria, Egypt, on the Mediterranean coast of the Nile Delta, was analyzed using SWMM 5.2 with its low impact development (LID) extension. The scenarios included four single-practice scenarios: green roof, permeable pavement, bioretention cell, and infiltration trench, each aimed at mitigating 20% of the impervious area, and three mixed portfolios with targets of 10%, 20%, and 30% impervious areas (MIX10, MIX20, MIX30). The catchment has an area-weighted imperviousness of 81.9%, and drainage is discharged from the tide gate to receive storm surge, astronomical tide, and sea-level rise (SLR) scenarios of +0.0, +0.5, and +1.0 m, together with an incrementally diminishing infiltration capacity due to rising shallow coastal groundwater levels. For a 10-year 2-hour return period design storm of 39.7 mm, baseline simulation provided 0.79 runoff coefficient, 14.09 m³/s of peak runoff, and 11,693 m³ of system flooding. Scenarios MIX30 reduced 27.9%, 35.1%, and 59.5% of runoff volume, peak runoff, and flood volume, respectively. Permeable pavement resulted in the largest flood volume reduction (56.9%) among single practices. Efficacy of GI systems decreased with an increase in storm size, as flood-volume reduction for MIX30 varied from 88.6% for a 2-year storm to 42.9% for a 50-year storm. A SLR scenario of +1.0 m increased baseline flooding by 17.1% and MIX30 flooding by 30.5%, hence decreasing the flood-volume reduction efficacy of MIX30 from 59.5% to 54.8%, including 204 m³ of water caused by limitations in infiltration associated with rising shallow groundwater level. Event loadings of total suspended solids (TSS), total nitrogen (TN), and total phosphorus (TP) were reduced with MIX30 by 44.4%, 40.5%, and 39.6%, respectively. papers.title: Soil erosion response to future climate variability and best management practices in the Kesinga catchment, India
papers.summary: Abstract Soil erosion poses a growing threat to watershed sustainability under changing climatic conditions, particularly in monsoon-dominated regions. This study integrates the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) with bias-corrected CORDEX–South Asia climate projections to quantify present and future sediment yield and to evaluate the effectiveness of structural best management practices (BMPs) in the Kesinga catchment, eastern India. The watershed was delineated into 33 sub-catchments, and model calibration and validation (2003–2020) demonstrated very good performance for streamflow during calibration (NSE = 0.86) and good performance during validation (NSE = 0.72). Sediment-yield performance was satisfactory during calibration (NSE = 0.52) but unsatisfactory during validation (NSE = 0.49), according to the performance criteria adopted in this study. Future projections under RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 scenarios indicate increases in streamflow (26–73%) and sediment yield (5–36%), with the greatest amplification under end-century RCP8.5 conditions; these sediment projections should be interpreted in light of the unsatisfactory validation performance. Spatial analysis revealed persistent sediment hotspots in central and eastern sub-catchments, where high slope gradients and projected precipitation intensification interact to enhance erosion risk. Across the future periods and scenarios, 40.2–51.2% of the catchment area was projected to fall within the severe-to-extreme erosion categories, with the highest proportion occurring under end-century RCP8.5. Structural BMPs, including grassed waterways (GWW) and vegetative filter strips (VFS), were implemented in priority sub-catchments. Under historical conditions, VFS and GWW reduced soil loss by 13% and 25%, respectively, while their combined application achieved up to 38% reduction. Although absolute sediment loads increased under future climates, combined BMP implementation consistently mitigated erosion by 27–36%, demonstra

papers.title: Landform-Based Evaluation of Settlement Distribution for Sustainable Spatial Planning in Badung Regency
authors: I Dewa Ayu Diah Citra Dewi
papers.summary: Badung Regency has experienced substantial development pressure over the past two decades, characterised by the conversion of agricultural land into built-up areas reaching hundreds of hectares per year, driven by tourism and residential expansion. The critical problem is that much development proceeds without regard to landform characteristics, escalating risks of flooding, erosion, landslides, and ecological degradation. Geomorphology-based assessments of the spatial distribution of built-up land remain scarce, despite offering greater comprehensiveness than conventional administrative zoning. This study aims to evaluate the distribution of built-up areas based on landform units in Badung Regency as a foundation for sustainable spatial planning. Methods include landform interpretation derived from Digital Elevation Model (DEM) data, the ESDM Geological Map, and spatial land-use data from the Geospatial Information Agency (BIG), supplemented by field surveys using purposive sampling across principal landform units. Results of landform delineation reveal that the study area comprises volcanic, denudational, fluvial, and marine landform units. Built-up expansion is predominantly concentrated on alluvial plains (F1), flood plains (F4), fluvial terraces (F14), and beach terraces (M4). Some development has encroached upon lower volcanic slopes and denudational hills, which are physically vulnerable. It is concluded that the distribution of built-up areas is not yet fully aligned with the physical carrying capacity of each landform unit, particularly fluvial and marine units characterised by high environmental sensitivity. Subsequent research is recommended to integrate multi-temporal Landsat imagery, historical disaster records encompassing floods, abrasion, landslides, and land subsidence, and climate change parameters to enhance the comprehensiveness and predictive capacity of landform-based suitability analysis.

papers.title: Blockage mechanisms of suspended particles in fractured ultra-low permeability reservoirs and optimization of water quality standards for post-fracturing injection
papers.summary: Abstract The ecological and environmental management department requires the treatment of oilfield produced water to comply with the "Technical Requirements and Analysis Methods for Water Quality Indicators of Clastic Rock Reservoir Water Injection" SY/T 5329 − 2022. The water quality indicators of oilfield injected water (mainly suspended solids content, median suspended solids particle size, petroleum content, etc.) are strictly required, and the above water quality indicators are mainly determined based on the actual permeability of the reservoir. Hydraulic fracturing creates complex "pore-fracture" dual-media systems in ultra-low permeability reservoirs, but the blockage mechanisms of suspended solids during post-fracturing water injection remain unclear—rendering conventional homogeneous-media water quality standards inadequate. Using core samples and Brazilian splitting to simulate fractures, this study reveals distinct blockage behaviors of particles and oil droplets in fractured media. A critical particle-to-pore-throat diameter ratio (PC = 1.059) is identified to quantitatively distinguish internal pore blockage from external filter cake formation, bridging classical bridging theory with practical diagnosis. Fractures exhibit a dual effect: they mitigate overall permeability damage as preferential flow pathways, yet enable deep invasion of solids and oil, complicating subsequent removal. Orthogonal experiments with proppants demonstrate that stringent Class I standards can be relaxed to Class IV (particle size≤5µm, concentration≤25mg/L, oil content≤30mg/L) while maintaining permeability loss below 25%. By clarifying fracture-induced blockage mechanisms and validating relaxed standards, this study provides theoretical insights and practical guidance for cost-effective water injection in fractured ultra-low permeability reservoirs.

Assessing the worthwhileness of efficiency enhancement methods mitigating buoyancy flow in high-temperature aquifer thermal energy storage
papers.summary: Abstract High-temperature aquifer thermal energy storage (HT-ATES) presents a promising approach for achieving a temporally and spatially balanced, continuous energy supply. A key challenge in HT-ATES systems is the density-driven buoyancy flow, which can result in considerable heat losses and reduced energy efficiency, or thermal recovery efficiency. This study explores two strategies for mitigating the effects of buoyancy flow: adjusting the working fluid’s salinity and modifying the production well screen length, under varying intensities of buoyancy flow. Numerical simulations are employed to evaluate the recovery efficiency and pumping energy requirements across a range of fluid salinities and screen lengths over multiple HT-ATES operational cycles. Under conditions of high intensity of buoyancy flow, the impact of different fluid salinities on thermal front evolution and associated hydrodynamic processes is analyzed. Recovery efficiency exhibits a nonmonotonic response to fluid salinity, with the maximum improvement reaching 36.5% at an increase in salinity of 6%. At a moderate intensity of buoyancy flow, altering fluid salinity proves ineffective due to the formation of a buffering layer, where cooled saline water separates the injected fluid from the surrounding groundwater. Comparatively, modifying fluid salinity is found to be more effective than adjusting the production well screen length. For both strategies, the additional pumping energy required is negligible relative to the gain in recovered heat. The number of operational cycles has minimal influence on the heat plume’s location and morphology. Furthermore, owing to the additional preferred pathways and irregular-shape fronts, the recovery efficiency enhancement methods are found more effective in heterogeneous aquifers.

papers.title: Shale‐Oil Micromigration and Sweet Spot Evaluation of the Shahejie Formation in the Dongying Sag, Bohai Bay Basin
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Strong heterogeneity of lacustrine shales in China hinders high‐precision shale‐oil sweet spot delineation, whereas the conventional “hydrocarbon generation‐retention” paradigm fails to account for widespread hydrocarbon micromigration. Here we systematically characterize micromigration in the Shahejie Formation shales from the Well NY1 of the Dongying Sag, Bohai Bay Basin, using Rock‐Eval pyrolysis, total organic carbon (TOC), and x‐ray diffraction (XRD) analysis, and establish a micromigration hydrocarbon ( δQ ) evaluation model. Results show widespread micromigration across the studied succession, with δQ values ranging from −523 to 559 mg/g TOC. Hydrocarbon intra‐micromigration (HIM) intervals account for 30.9% of the section and exhibit significantly higher oil content ( S 1 ) and oil mobility (quantified by the oil saturation index [OSI]) relative to hydrocarbon extra‐micromigration (HEM) intervals. Multiple geochemical evidences support micromigration, including suppressed T max values, abnormally elevated production index at low thermal maturity, and selective enrichment of light saturated hydrocarbon fractions in HIM intervals. Carbonate‐rich lithofacies are identified as preferential sites for hydrocarbon charging, whereas intervals with high TOC and high original hydrogen index tend to act as hydrocarbon expulsion zones. Mineral assemblages exert primary controls on micromigration pathways and efficiency via modulation of pore structure, capillary pressure, and rock brittleness. On this basis, we develop an improved sweet spot criterion by integrating the micromigration parameter δQ with conventional indicators ( S 1 and OSI). Application of this criterion identifies four Type I sweet spot intervals (3382–3394, 3408–3413, 3444–3468, and 3480–3500 m) in the Well NY1. This study confirms the role of hydrocarbon micromigration in differential shale‐oil enrichment in lacustrine basins and provides a quantitative method for micromigration type sweet s

papers.title: Bridging Laboratory and Field Performance in Copper Sulfide Bio-Heap Leaching: Critical Evaluation of Bottle-Roll, Column, and Pilot Testing
papers.source: Journal International Review of Research Studies
papers.summary: Laboratory extraction profiles from copper sulfide bioleaching are frequently treated as predictors of heap performance. However, the experimental regimes differ in wetting, gas access, thermal inertia, microbial attachment, and mineralogical heterogeneity. This critical review evaluates the transferability of evidence across bottle-roll or stirred tests, packed columns, large columns, pilot heaps, and commercial operations. The synthesis integrates the supplied bibliography, explicitly distinguishing copper-specific evidence, mechanistic evidence from acidophilic systems, and transferable analogies from other leaching ores. Bottle tests are useful for preliminary reaction screening but cannot resolve preferential flow or gravity drainage; columns introduce coupled liquid–gas transport, whereas pilot heaps are needed to test the persistence of aeration, solution distribution, and thermal gradients under more representative boundary conditions. The proposed framework treats scale-up as preservation of coupled mechanisms, not replication of an isolated recovery percentage. A tiered evidence ladder, scale-fidelity matrix, and decision gates guide the design, reporting, and interpretation of industrially relevant test programs.

Prioritizing Fuel Treatments to Reduce Post-Fire Debris Flow Risk in Utah
papers.summary: Wildfire is a natural part of many forest ecosystems, but in the western United States, wildfires have become larger, more frequent, and more severe in recent decades. There are serious problems after severe wildfire, including erosion, flooding, and debris flows that threaten water quality, roads, and communities. Because of this, land managers need better ways to decide where fuel treatments, such as prescribed burning or thinning, can most effectively reduce wildfire damage and post-fire risks. In this dissertation, I studied how fuel treatments might reduce wildfire severity and lower the risk of post-fire debris flows in Utah. First, I built a model to predict how severely forests are likely to burn across the state. Next, I used simulated treatment scenarios to test how different fuel treatments changed wildfire severity in different forest types and under different weather conditions. Finally, I applied those results to real watersheds in Utah to estimate how treatments could reduce post-fire debris-flow risk. The results showed that treatment effectiveness depends strongly on forest type. In some forests, especially ponderosa pine, spruce-fir, and lodgepole pine, reducing fuels had a strong effect on lowering fire severity. In other forest types, weather played a larger role, which made treatments less effective. Across most forests, treatments that reduced both canopy fuels and surface fuels produced the greatest reductions in wildfire severity. At the watershed scale, treatment costs and benefits also varied. Prescribed burning was generally the most cost-effective treatment. In several watersheds, including Electric Lake, Big Cottonwood Canyon, Panguitch Lake, and Rockport, cost-effective treatments provided the greatest reduction in post-fire risk for the money invested, making them especially important areas for management. Other watersheds showed less cost-benefit tradeoffs in decision making, where intensive treatments can be prioritized for maximal b

papers.title: Non-eruptive debris flows at Mount Shasta: historical record, drivers, and implications for future hazards
papers.summary: Assessments of water-driven mass flows at snow and ice-covered volcanoes are often based on the assumption that the most impactful flows will happen during eruptions (lahars). However, as eruptions are a relatively low-probability event, non-eruptive debris flows tied to precipitation or glacial outburst floods may be more common. This is especially relevant at Mount Shasta, one of the southernmost glaciated stratovolcanoes in the Cascade volcanic arc, where past hazards assessments focused on the possibility of larger flows triggered by eruptive activity. Recent years (2021–2025) at Mount Shasta, however, have seen smaller non-eruptive lahars (locally called ‘debris flows’), which have had significant impacts on the communities and infrastructure surrounding the volcano, disrupting major transportation routes and threatening municipal water supplies. Given Mount Shasta’s current quiescence, it is prudent to focus volcanic hazard assessment on these non-eruptive lahars. In this study, we expand the historical record of debris flow occurrence and determine whether there is a discernible link between debris flow frequency and broader, meteorological forces. We classify debris flows into two broad groups based on associated meteorological parameters: (1) flows triggered by rainfall during storms, and (2) flows without associated precipitation occurring during hot summer days in years with widespread drought, including below average snow accumulation in the previous winter. These findings are consistent with historical anecdotal observations by local residents – that debris flow occurrence outside of precipitation is more frequent in hot, dry summers – and provide important information for evaluating which meteorological conditions may lead to an increase in debris flow occurrence. We also highlight the fact that debris flows may be a hazard at Mount Shasta even when there is no precipitation. These results provide important data for evaluating debris flow hazards in th

papers.title: Linking Hydrodynamic Transport and Nutrient Fluxes to Land‐Use Patterns: A Predictive Framework for Soil Conservation in a Mountainous Catchment
papers.summary: ABSTRACT This study investigates the influence of land use on total suspended solids (TSS) flux and nutrient leaching within a mixed land‐use catchment. The primary objective was to enhance predictive accuracy for soil erosion and water quality by assessing hydrologic drivers critical for managing degradation risks. Our findings demonstrate a significant land‐use impact: stream reaches adjacent to arable land exhibited the highest concentrations of nitrate nitrogen (up to 6.25 mg dm −3 ) and phosphates (0.89 mg dm −3 ), whereas forests and permanent grasslands showed significantly lower levels. Arable lands also recorded the highest transport intensity (1.02 m 3 s −1 ), reflecting increased surface runoff and diminished water retention capacity compared to forested reaches (0.47 m 3 s −1 ). Furthermore, the complete transverse mixing distance, a proxy for natural purification efficiency, was longest in arable‐dominated reaches (52.26 m), contrasting with shorter distances in forests (35.26 m) and grasslands (31.21 m). Spatial autoregression (SAR) modeling identified significant correlations between phosphate levels and agricultural zones, as well as nitrate nitrogen and grasslands. These results underscore the necessity of integrating land‐use management into forest engineering and maintaining permanent riparian grasslands to optimize nutrient retention and sediment control in erosion‐prone regions.

Modelling coupled flow and morphodynamics in lahars
papers.summary: Lahars are one of the most dangerous volcanic hazards, with rapid onset and multiple potential sources. Flows can occur syn-eruptively, or for years post-eruption as catchments on volcanic flanks adjust to the changes in sediment supply, land cover and topography following eruptions. As multiphase mixtures of water, volcaniclastic sediments and entrained debris, with solids content evolving in space and time and spanning hyperconcentrated to debris flow regimes, lahars remain challenging to model. We present a shallow-layer model of lahars, that includes a novel phenomenological description of flow resistance that varies between turbulent and granular behaviours with the changing solids content. This provides a pragmatic representation of lahar dynamics across hyperconcentrated and debris flow regimes. Evolution of the solids content is modelled through suspended sediment transport, entrainment through bed erosion, and hindered settling of the solid phase. We couple the morphodynamics and hydrodynamics through bed shear stresses and deposition rates, allowing for temporally evolving topography. Through numerical model simulations in an idealised geometry, we illustrate the coupling between the hydro- and morpho-dynamics and identify three regimes: (i) a stable morphodynamic equilibrium, (ii) local self-channelization, and (iii) a “super-erosive” regime for which a sediment-rich flow front forms from excavation of bed sediments. We examine the predictive capability of the model against observations of lahars and non-volcanic debris flows. Detailed measurement of the dynamics of rainfall-triggered lahars in the Cenizas channel at Fuego, Guatemala, have been acquired by instrumenting the channel with video cameras, seismic stations and acoustic (infrasound) arrays, allowing us to estimate flow velocities, infer changes in solids content, and observe evolution of the channel morphology.
